content: Elon Musk said AI companies may soon run into serious cash shortages as they wait for revenue-generating data centers to come online. The SpaceX and Tesla CEO replied to an X post on Saturday that showed comparatively low stock valuations for semiconductor manufacturers, relative to their expected profits. This could suggest that investors are bearish on AI-powering chip companies continuing to notch soaring profits in the race for compute — a sign that data center construction may face serious headwinds in the near future. "The cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year," Musk said, adding that delays in data center activations would require "hundreds of billions" in more capital for AI companies. "Where will that come from?" he asked. Tech stocks in US markets took it on the chin last week. The S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory on Friday, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from recent highs. The market carnage prompted some to speculate that the AI bubble had popped. Financial regulators in semiconductor-heavy Taiwan on Saturday said they would limit short selling — an action similar to one taken by US regulators during the 2008 housing crisis. Though leading AI and AI-adjacent companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic are reporting growing revenue, they're also spending massive sums to secure compute — powered by key hardware that enables chatbots and other AI tools. Compute is largely provided by data centers, which have faced their own series of setbacks recently, from backlash from the communities where they are being built to the blue midterm wave and construction delays. And without a reliable network of data centers, AI companies are hobbled in their ability to scale to meet investor demand. Data center operators, meanwhile, are left at the altar with their multibillion-dollar investments failing to generate revenue. "Getting this amount of compute turned on, cooled and working reliably is incredibly hard," Musk said. Jump to

Ffion, Yugraj and Jessica say being ghosted has become a common part of applying for jobs  Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer? So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work. It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training -  those dubbed as Neets - this week.  Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback". The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems. But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market? Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July. But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person". He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not." Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications. The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.  Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview. "With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says. Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation. The Milburn report, external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications. "It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon. Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them. And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.  But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this.  Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says. "It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says. The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting.  But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect? Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best. Ellie says constructive feedback is always preferable to being ghosted  "If you are applying for hundreds of jobs and never getting anything, I think something is going wrong... You can't fix something unless you know what the problem is." There are things applicants can do to improve their chances and avoid ghosting, such as tailoring their CV to each job and not submitting "hundreds and hundreds of applications" that all look the same, Burton adds. Candidates should also never take being ghosted personally, she adds.  "Not hearing back doesn't mean you aren't a great candidate. Put it down to experience and move on." When I got the keys to my house in 2021, it was far from perfect. Damp seeped through the walls, electrical wires dangled from the ceilings, and the windows were rusted shut. Thankfully, I didn't buy it for the questionable workmanship or bizarre style choices — I chose it for its incredible potential. It was also very cheap for the area, and we paid $342,000. Located on the edge of a thriving district in the North of England, the house was a larger-than-average semi-detached converted mill store with solid stone walls, valley views, and a curved driveway. Set across three stories, it was somewhere I could see as a forever home for my partner and me, as well as the baby I was pregnant with at the time. As soon as we moved in, the scaffolding went up, and we set to work having the roof redone and the stone repointed. The outside of the house was the most expensive and time-consuming part of the renovation, as it required skilled stone masons to restore the walls and roof tiles by hand. Once they did that, the damp inside started to dry out, so we stripped out the internal walls and replaced them. Every time we started a new job, we would find another issue — the plumbing hadn't been connected properly, or there were electric sockets without power. The work had been done so badly the first time around that we had to redo everything the previous owners had attempted. We considered it a labor of love, so while the baby slept, we dug out piles of dumped rocks from the garden and replaced the broken fences with traditional stone ones. Even though it was a lot of hard labor, we felt it would be worth it. When I was back at work, we redesigned the entire kitchen, which had been built next to the damp wall, so new units had to be fitted to the other side. We also had window shutters, flooring, bathrooms, and cupboards installed, which meant that two stories were complete. None of this was cheap, but it was unrecognizable from what had been before, and the neighbors loved it. It was once we reached the third and final floor that renovation fatigue set in. We got permission to change the layout, but finding builders was hard, and it required a lot of paperwork. As it had to be done in stages, it took over a year to complete, and we couldn't use it for months. That's when we decided to sell once it was completed. Thankfully, we hadn't gone very far over budget, as we'd spent $200,000 in total. However, it wasn't money that was the issue; it was our exhaustion with the constant stress of it all. We'd had another baby by this point, and it was becoming harder to keep everything in 'perfect' condition. The house had become a job to us, and even with the finish line in sight, it just didn't feel like a home anymore. It was like living in a showroom, and I didn't have the energy to maintain it. After putting so much effort into it over those five years, the doubts built up. Were we sure this was where we wanted to be? Was this definitely the best place for the kids? Did we still think this was our forever home? The answer was no to all of them. Once the last tradesperson had left, we put it on the market straightaway, despite having a tiny baby and a 4-year-old. Luckily for us, buyers loved the house and the work we'd put into it, so we made a small profit, selling it for $647,000. Still, the renovations had taken so much effort that it was a tiny wage for the hours we had put in. Once it was sold, I felt free. I'd spent all my time clearing up dust and chasing tradesmen, as well as solving endless problems, which was a burden on top of raising young kids and holding down a job. Now we live in a cottage a few miles from our old place, and we're much happier. The experience has taught me that home isn't about how it looks but how you feel about it. Jump to

AIAi slopAtariRetroSteven SpielbergVideo Game Industry  While the underlying cause for the 1983 video game crash is contested by historians, the culture has always singled out one particular culprit. Based on Spielbergâs blockbuster film, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrialâs Atari adaptation was a dud. Soon after, the industry collapsed in on itself, with many blaming store shelves overburdened with lazily made slop. Now, the gameâs original programmer is warning that the crash could repeat itself, this time with AI to blame instead of E.T. Speaking at the DevGAMM conference in Lisbon, vetted game designer Howard Scott Warshaw gave a warning. “You ever hear of the crash of ’83 or ’84, the big video game crash?” said Warshaw. “They said the problem that happened in the crash, and I think that was true, was there was a glut of crap on the market, because the machine opened up and anybody could just pop a game out, and they didâ¦ AI is going to have the same impact on a larger scale, because on the one level, so many more people can now realise and create a video game than ever could before just using AI.” In the early â80s, there were a lot of home consoles, a lot of software between them, and a lot of confused parents. As the quality between these games were spread thinner, consumers’ patience wore out. Warshaw already had hit games under his belt, such as the classic Yarâs Revenge, but when Atari approached him about adapting the hit E.T., released just that summer, they only gave him a few weeks to make the holiday season. The game was an indecipherable mess. Kids who were excited to ‘phone home’ discovered something that felt ‘phoned in.’ Expecting to ride the filmâs runaway success, there were so many unsold copies that urban legends emerged that most of them were secretly buried in a ditch in New Mexico. An urban legend that turned out to be true. Warshaw says that through the late â70s and early â80s, critics were eager to call video games a fad. Many of his peers were worried the crash proved them right, sending the signal to investors and industry to pull the money out. On the other side of the world, Nintendo was readying to expand to the global market. They took a lot of notes from the competitionsâ failures. The NES was designed around avoiding another crash. Simplified, VCR-like design and cartridges, with strict quality control on software developers that would create more rivals than partners in the long run. Today, no oneâs calling video games a fad. Outside of the occasional cable pundit, few confuse the major consoles or deny the cultural footprint of Grand Theft Auto. But elements of the â80s crash are replaying in other, frustrating ways. Warshaw isnât a hardliner against AI. He says it can speed up the coding process exponentially. But heâs also aware, well aware, that with that speed comes sloppiness. And while most shelves are digital instead of brick and mortar, seeing them stocked with shit will have the same underlying effect. “There’s some things in life that everybody can see themselves doing, and the truth is most people who do it can’t do it very well,” says Warshaw. “What AI is going to do is make that more possible for people who can’t do it to do itâ¦ We need better filters to figure out a way to get rid of the garbage games and not waste time with that, and to highlight what are really innovative and exciting things.” Digital storefronts have been bodied by an influx of hastily-made, AI-produced slop. Steam, who traditionally allow the market to dictate its frontpage, is well aware of how gaudy their feed has become. itch.io, also being buried with machine-made crud, has taken a more direct approach by deleting more than a terabyte of the stuff. The trend risks far more than eye rolls. Across the board, these storefronts are being inundated with AI-created junk, but their sales are disproportionately non-existent compared to human-made offerings. Discoverability has long been a problem on these platforms, but if the trend continues towards hosting unsellable, automatic shovelware burying legitimate games, these pages could face a legitimate monetary crisis. Ideally, Warshaw says this trend will reemphasize a focus on design. That AI will encourage creative attention towards elements that the tech cannot produce itself. But as many contemporary game makers will note, genius is seldom rewarded by these platforms. If these current grievances are merely a stress test on the future to come, platforms will need to rethink their philosophy, lest they start digging holes in Alamogordo. Compass and Usona are vying for an FDA first, but pricing, payer coverage and patient access could determine the commercial winner. The race to win the first FDA nod for a classic psychedelic just got more interesting. Compass Pathways has long been dubbed a leader of the field with its psilocybin-based candidate for treatment-resistant depression, considered the furthest along in development and predicted to become a blockbuster. But a dark horse recently sprang from the gate amid reports it beat Compass to the FDA with its psilocybin drug in depression. Usona Institute, a nonprofit based in Wisconsin, has mostly kept a low profile about its investigational psilocybin candidate PSIL201. In March 2024, it launched its phase 3 trial for the treatment. By April this year, the FDA said Usona’s treatment had secured a voucher for a speedier review under the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher Program. Then earlier this month, a psychedelics industry analyst reported that Usona had already filed for FDA approval, a revelation that “caught many investors by surprise,” analysts at Stifel said in a note.  Usona hasn’t confirmed the FDA submission and in an emailed statement to PharmaVoice said it is not providing comments at this time. But the unconfirmed reports have already had a ripple effect.  Shares of Compass dropped by around 30% following the news. A week later, Compass announced it completed its own approval application. And now analysts are reconfiguring their picture of how the market could take shape.  Is Compass’ candidate, COMP360, still projected to become a blockbuster? Yes, multiple analysts predict. But will it rule the market alone? Here are the dynamics Compass will have to navigate.  In most circumstances, it wouldn’t look like Usona has the goods to deliver on an FDA nod. Two pivotal trials are often used to support FDA approval, and Usona has yet to publicly release data from its phase 3 study. The trial's six-week double-blind treatment period might also fall short of the FDA's expectations for longer-term blinded data, Stifel analysts noted.  Then again, the regulatory landscape could come to Usona’s rescue.  “Beyond the broader push from HHS towards approval and access for psychedelic medicines, the current head of CDER, Michael Davis, was previously employed at Usona,” the analysts noted.  At the same time, Compass also has reasons to believe Usona won’t become a direct competitor even if its drug is approved. Usona has been studying its candidate in major depressive disorder — a distinct indication from treatment-resistant depression.  Usona’s mission is also to supply psilocybin at a low cost that provides broad access. Compass, on the other hand, has won several patents for COMP360 and is more likely to price it in line with new branded drugs, according to Emma Wille, a senior analyst at Norstella’s Citeline.  In a market forecast published in August 2026, Wille estimated a drug list price of about $34,000 per year for COMP360, based on the Compass-guided estimate of two to four doses per year.  Although sales projections for COMP360 would depend on pricing and dosing frequency, Stifel analysts noted that it “only takes small penetration in this market to get close to blockbuster status.” Analysts at RBC Capital Markets concurred with the blockbuster prediction, writing in a note that despite potential competitors, COMP360 could reach $1.9 billion in peak sales in treatment-resistant depression alone, and that there is “sufficient room for many new psychedelics” — a conclusion with which Wille agreed.  But getting payers on board and securing patient access will be key.  The terms of payer coverage will be one of the main hurdles, Wille said.  In order to get a new depression treatment approved, patients will likely have to try — and not respond to — at least a few generic medications. That dynamic is already intrinsic in the treatment-resistant depression indication Compass is targeting. It’s also the same treatment arena where Johnson & Johnson’s esketamine spray Spravato won approval and soared to blockbuster heights. But Spravato has an additional edge.  “Spravato also has that extra approval for acute suicidality, which might scoot patients toward Spravato sooner,” Wille said, while noting that this probably only happens in rare cases based on conversations she’s had with physicians about prescribing patterns.  COMP360 is also more complex to administer than the currently approved depression treatments, requiring multiple hours of in-clinic time with trained professionals.  To get payers on board, Compass is likely to lean on its treatment’s durability, Wille said. In September, Compass released new, longer-term phase 3 data for COMP360, touting its durability for patients on various dosing schedules after 52 weeks.  “Across the 52-week study period, participants experienced cumulative and sustained reductions in depressive symptoms,” the company said in a release. While it is still unclear how often patients would be dosed with COMP360 if it’s approved, it’s unlikely to be more than a few times a year, Wille said, which could make payers more open to covering it. “The idea of having a treatment for this chronic disorder that you may only need two or three times a year … that’s very attractive to patients. And it’s attractive to payers,” Wille said.  As these dynamics play out, Compass will be doing a lot of the “initial grunt work” for the wider pharma industry by navigating how to bring a classic psychedelic drug to market and get it to patients, Wille said. And that market is set to potentially expand in the coming years as companies like Definium Therapeutics and AtaiBeckley, which was recently acquired by Eli Lilly, advance their psychedelic-based candidates through the clinic for various psychiatric indications.  “What we’re learning from these psilocybin NDAs and the way the FDA responds and what we hear about payer coverage … is just going to be the building blocks toward potentially someday having a healthcare system that supports this type of treatment,” Wille said.  Get the free daily newsletter read by industry leaders Compass and Usona are vying for an FDA first, but pricing, payer coverage and patient access could determine the commercial winner. Democrats should also support Jeffries' House speaker nomination, Emanuel said. Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel said Sunday that longtime Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer should commit to stepping down from the role after the next Congress, where Democrats are set to hold 56 seats after a strong midterm election showing. "If I was Chuck Schumer, what I would say is, 'I'm going to secure the majority, I am not going to run for majority leader next cycle, and I'm going to make sure the other -- the young voices and faces of this party grow. That would take that tension out of this," Emanuel, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said on ABC's "This Week." "So he should serve as majority leader for these next two years?" co-anchor Jonathan Karl followed up. "Yeah, just get it over with," Emanuel said. "Chuck Schumer is a friend, as is [Sen.] Chris Van Hollen, but this is not what people voted for. They voted to get their lives better, not yours." Emanuel, who also served as U.S. ambassador to Japan under President Joe Biden and chief of staff to President Barack Obama, has previously called for instituting a mandatory retirement age of 75 for federal public officials, including members of Congress. Schumer turns 76 on Monday. Van Hollen announced on Nov. 14 he was officially challenging Schumer for the role of majority leader in the congressional session beginning in January. On last Sunday's episode of "This Week," Van Hollen told co-anchor Martha Raddatz that maintaining the status quo is not how Democrats will "earn the people's trust." The vote for majority leader, which is a secret ballot, is scheduled for Dec. 1. While Democrats’ Senate leader is still undecided, House Democrats voted Wednesday to officially nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York to be their candidate for speaker of the House. If he wins a majority of votes among all House members in January, as he’s expected to do, he will become the first Black speaker in U.S. history. Nearly all Democrats supported Jeffries’ nomination, but there were 11 defectors. Of the eight individuals ABC News has confirmed voted against his candidacy, all were elected for the first time in November. Emanuel had a message to Jeffries’ naysayers, most of whom identify with the progressive wing of the party, including some who are democratic socialists: “Give me a break.” “Hakeem Jeffries is history, OK? … First Black speaker, number two in line for the presidency. And as somebody who was chief of staff to President Obama, that is a statement about America that we should take pride in,” Emanuel said. “We're a coalition. You're going to tell the most loyal coalition partner, the African American community, that the moment in history, you're not going to get it?” "The Black vote is the most significant, most loyal, most dedicated part of the coalition," Emanuel continued. "You voted against Hakeem Jeffries, who made history and earned it when we were in the minority. You just came along and literally hadn't earned this election. He literally over the years built a majority here that should be affirmed and not only affirmed. It tells me when you vote against him, you don't understand the politics of the Democratic Party.” Emanuel outlined lofty policy goals he thinks the incoming Democratic majorities should try to achieve, including raising the federal hourly minimum wage to $20 by 2030 and reducing or completely undoing tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump. He also called for a major ethics reform package that would impact all three branches of government. “Ban all stock trading … ban all prediction market participation. Mandatory blind trust, mandatory age and term limit mark out, and what I call the Jared Kushner rule: no foreign money while you're in and for two years out of government,” Emanuel said. Karl also asked Emanuel what he thinks the next Democratic president should do about the still-under-construction White House ballroom that has been one of the president’s prized projects this term. The White House has said the goal is to finish it before Trump leaves office. “I think the opening floor should be dedicated to the history of our democracy and what we built: the good, the bad, the ugly,” Emanuel said. “And so you have a version of what the president has done, which is -- I think is horrendous, both substantively and in style that he did, but dedicate a major portion as you walk in, the guests will walk in, to the democracy of this country.” Emanuel also said that the Rose Garden, which Trump turned into a stone patio, should be reverted back to the design that dates back to the Kennedy administration. As for whether he'll seek the Democratic presidential nomination for 2028, Emanuel was tight-lipped. "When do you make this decision-slash-announcement?" Karl asked. "As soon as I get out of here," Emanuel quipped. 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

From  By          Jackie Fortiér                        A counselor, right, helps a client through the Medicare signup process at a resource center for older adults in Sunrise, Florida. Medicare open enrollment season started Oct. 15 and ends Dec. 7.                                                           Joe Cavaretta/South Florida Sun Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images  hide caption  Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential. Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year. Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one plan. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu. Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services. Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning. As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums. "People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy. Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn't tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.                  About 4 million people are in Medicare Advantage plans that won't be offered in 2027. If they do nothing, they'll be automatically enrolled in traditional Medicare.                                                           Jenny Kane/AP                                       hide caption  Some beneficiaries who didn't have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt tospread out over the course of the year. Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don't shop around could be leaving money on the table. "It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027," she said. An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they'll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it's important to read the fine print and add up the other costs. "There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide," Lipschutz said. So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover? And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027. "Look at that dollar value specifically," she said. For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won't come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a late-enrollment penalty on their monthly premiums for life. When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don't pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage. If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York are exceptions. Enrollees whose Advantage plans have not been renewed — and haven't been consolidated into another plan — can switch to traditional Medicare and buy a Medigap policy without a health screening, but they need to act before March. Medicare experts advise enrollees to write down all their prescription drugs, as well as any procedures planned in the next year, such as a joint replacement or dental work, to help them decide which plan will cover their needs. Call a favorite doctor's office to see whether they are in-network for the plans being considered. Remember that brokers might earn commissions, especially on Advantage plans, and might not represent every plan. For unbiased help, every state has a federally funded State Health Insurance Assistance Program that offers free plan counseling specific to your situation, in person and over the phone. To get help, go to the website at shiphelp.org/open-enrollment, email info@shiphelp.org, or call the SHIP National Technical Assistance Center at 877-839-2675. A SHIP counselor can also help enrollees apply for benefits that help pay for Medicare premiums and prescription drug costs, such as the Medicare Savings Programs and Medicare Part D Extra Help. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ryan Chaw, a 34-year-old who quit his job as a pharmacist and now lives off rental income from his 12 properties. Chaw, who lives in Sacramento, California, bought his first property at 23 years old and rented it out by the room. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Early in life, I realized that investing in real estate was the best way to create generational wealth. My grandpa bought a set of flats in the San Francisco Bay Area, and not only was he able to retire early, but he also was able to support me and my brother through college. Back in the 1950s, the properties were dirt cheap, but as time went on, those properties went up in value tremendously, and the rents went up as well. When my parents eventually sold my grandpa's properties after he passed away, they sold them for about $3.6 million.  That was more money than they made in their entire lives. They worked 40 hours a week, essentially, for 30 years while this single set of flats in San Francisco sat for the same amount of time, and they made more with the flats. It put things into perspective for me: work smarter, not harder. So I became obsessed with that concept, and I had a really good example. Still, it was scary to dive into real estate investing. It's intimidating to get into something you've never done before and know nothing about.  I wasn't taking much action on buying a house. I was talking about buying rentals a lot, and my dad called me out and said, "Hey Ryan, you seem to be talking about rentals, but I haven't seen you even contact a real estate agent yet. Isn't that the first step?" I remember at the time I kind of got angry, more at myself. That same day, I called a real estate agent, drove down to Stockton, California, which is about an hour away from me, and saw three or four properties. I put an offer on one of the properties that same day.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  I didn't know what I was doing. It was a $262,000 house, but I put down $100,000 for my down payment because I didn't know that the normal down payment people put down is 20%. My first house was literally across the street from the University of Pacific (UOP). It was maybe a one- to two-minute walk from the school library. I figured I would already have a lot of high demand constantly — I heard location is the most important thing in real estate. I rented to college students, and I figured that all college students care about is how close they are to their classes; that's the most important thing for them. And I was right. In my very first year, I didn't know how to market, so I had some trouble getting the first few rooms filled. But after the first year, I had zero vacancy. It was rent-by-the-room, and there were three bedrooms at first, but then I learned that if I added extra bedrooms, I could make much more rental income. The rental income about covered my mortgage, but then I added a fourth bedroom, and it was making cash flow. I started charging about $630 per room, but it slowly went up to about $720 over the years. My mortgage was about $2,000 a month. I took out a 10-year mortgage and was actually able to pay it off completely after five years. I bought my second property the following year. I basically made a point to buy one property per year. With the second property, I didn't have money to buy it because I was using so much money to pay for repairs on my first home — my pharmacist salary was good, but it wasn't that good. I had to be creative on the second property because I didn't have enough cash or a full 20% down. I had to put 10% down. I bought it as a second home based on the advice from my lender, so I had to live in it for a certain amount of time.  Outside of that, I lived with my parents rent-free for the first five years and bought one property a year. The first five houses were all investment, rent-by-the-room properties right next to UOP, all in the same area. The sixth one I bought, I moved into and did a house hack. I read "Rich Dad Poor Dad," and I was really inspired by the idea of buying assets that generate income that puts money in your pocket, and eventually that money in your pocket can replace your income. I was kind of a follower of the FIRE and financial independence movements. I figured that if I could replace my pharmacist salary and make about $10,000 a month from my rentals, I would feel comfortable leaving the pharmacist position. It took me about eight years to get there. I started at the end of 2015 and resigned in August 2023. My first house was a 100-year-old house, and it had a lot of things that broke down on it, and it was only four bedrooms. Obviously, the five-bedroom and six-bedroom properties give you more cash flow. Even though it was paid off and cash-flowing, I wanted to expand to a market that had a higher cash flow overall. So I started buying out of state. I sold my first home for $437,500, and I used that money to put it into Ohio properties. I bought seven Ohio properties, like, for example, a duplex that makes about $4,000 a month in cash flow. I bought it for $367,000. I still have four other properties in Stockton, one in Sacramento, and now I have seven in Ohio. I eventually want to own 100 properties. Real estate definitely isn't the only way to get wealthy. My grandpa was also a big investor in stocks. I think that's a way to build your wealth, but it's not a way to build passive income as easily. The real estate method can lead to financial freedom in a very predictable, consistent way. Managing a small portfolio of five properties to make six figures is kind of like the dream, right? And a lot of people can get there. I still have my pharmacist license, but I don't have to work. I haven't actually gone back to working as a pharmacist since 2023. It's not like I didn't enjoy pharmacy; it was a great means, and it provided a really good stepping stone for me. I might go back to working one or two days a week on the weekends or something, but I don't have to. And I think the freedom to be able to choose that was what I was aiming for. Jump to

Home                                                                                      >              Journals                                                         >              Michigan Law Review                                                         >              MLR                                     >              Volume 118                                                                   >              Issue 7 (2020)  The recent revival of political interest in antitrust has resurfaced a longstanding debate about the role of industrial concentration and monopoly in enabling Hitler’s rise to power and the Third Reich’s wars of aggression. Proponents of stronger antitrust enforcement argue that monopolies and cartels brought the Nazis to power and warn that rising concentration in the American economy could similarly threaten democracy. Skeptics demur, observing that German big business largely opposed Hitler during the crucial years of his ascent. Drawing on business histories and archival material from the U.S. Office of Military Government’s Decartelization Branch, this Article assesses the historical record on the role of industrial concentration in facilitating Nazism. It finds compelling evidence that, while German big business principally did not support Hitler before he won the chancellorship in 1933, the extreme concentration of market power during the Weimar period enabled Hitler to seize and consolidate totalitarian power through a variety of mechanisms. Hence, the German experience with Nazism lends support to the idea that extreme concentration of economic power enables extreme concentration of political power. However, most of the conduct that created the radical economic concentration of the Weimar period would be unlawful under contemporary antitrust principles, which casts doubt on claims that a significant shift in antitrust enforcement is necessary to forestall antidemocratic forces. The chipmaker has lost roughly $1.7 trillion in market capitalization since the slide began in early October, a 30% decline that pushed the company below Apple in market value [1][5]. The drop was the stock's worst weekly performance since April 2025 [1][5]. The decline accelerated after co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Nov. 12, Thursday, following the disclosure of two separate extramarital affairs [5]. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent successor [5]. The events capped a sharp reversal for a company that had spent most of the year as the world's most valuable publicly traded firm. Nvidia recently reported quarterly results, with analysts projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to the London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG). The report was the first since Huang's departure and comes as the company navigates both leadership uncertainty and a broader pullback in artificial intelligence-related equities.Market Selloff Began Before Huang Resignation Investors turned bearish on Nvidia before the recent leadership crisis. Selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, but the stock was already in a downward slide that began in early October [5]. Before Huang's exit, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%, with much of that decline coming after midterm elections that produced sweeping Democratic victories and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout [5]. In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock had been sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is highly profitable, major customers such as neocloud providers rely heavily on debt markets to fund their expansion [5]. Those dynamics weighed on the entire semiconductor sector [1]. The selloff has not been confined to Nvidia. Asian chipmakers also fell sharply, with Taiwan's Taiex dropping 6% and South Korea's Kospi losing 4%, according to ZeroHedge [1]. The declines came as the Financial Times reported that ousted Huang is discussing a comeback, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent demanded a dramatic shakeup and an outside CEO.Huang Resigns After Affairs Become Public Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led the company for 33 years, resignedÂ Nov. 12,Â after two separate extramarital affairs were disclosed [5]. One affair was with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with a company employee. The board convened late Nov. 11 after the Times reported on the second affair, this one with the company's vice president of health care. By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world. News of the first reported affair hit front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife [5]." Market participants had initially treated the scandal as company-specific. That assessment shifted as the second affair became public and the board moved quickly to install interim leadership [5].Board Names Interim CEO, Analyst Reacts The board named Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a full-time successor, reported Nvidia. Kress, who has served as the company's chief financial officer since 2013, takes over at a critical juncture. Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report that the departure creates a challenging transition. "With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang, we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Luria wrote. He lowered his price target to $200 from $300 but maintained a buy rating on the stock [5]. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," added Luria [5]. The leadership change comes as Nvidia faces increasing competition in the AI chip market. The company has pursued strategic deals to maintain its dominance, including a $20 billion licensing agreement for Groq's AI technology aimed at countering Google's growing influence in inference hardware [2].Earnings Report and Analyst Outlook Nvidia recently reported quarterly results. Analysts have projected 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion. That figure is up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report that even though they expect the company to report solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term." The departure of Mr. Huang could translate to a lingering share overhang, they added [5]. The firm maintained its outperform rating on the stock. The broader context for Nvidia's report includes a market that has grown increasingly skeptical of the artificial intelligence trade. Industry projections suggest AI-related infrastructure spending could exceed $5 trillion by 2030, with data center capacity demand reaching 100 gigawatts, according to estimates cited in industry reports [3]. Whether Nvidia can meet those expectations amid leadership uncertainty remains an open question.Conclusion: Pressure on Interim CEO as Nvidia Moves Forward Kress faces immediate pressure as interim CEO after the earnings report, according to analysts. Oppenheimer's assessment that the departure could translate to a lingering share overhang suggests the market may need more than one earnings beat to regain confidence. The stock's longer-term direction will depend on company performance and market conditions, officials and analysts indicated. Nvidia stock suffers longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.7 trillion. https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-stock-jensen-affair-ai.html     In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock had been sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is highly profitable, major customers such as neocloud providers rely heavily on debt markets to fund their expansion [5]. Those dynamics weighed on the entire semiconductor sector [1]. The selloff has not been confined to Nvidia. Asian chipmakers also fell sharply, with Taiwan's Taiex dropping 6% and South Korea's Kospi losing 4%, according to ZeroHedge [1]. The declines came as the Financial Times reported that ousted Huang is discussing a comeback, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent demanded a dramatic shakeup and an outside CEO.Huang Resigns After Affairs Become Public Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led the company for 33 years, resignedÂ Nov. 12,Â after two separate extramarital affairs were disclosed [5]. One affair was with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with a company employee. The board convened late Nov. 11 after the Times reported on the second affair, this one with the company's vice president of health care. By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world. News of the first reported affair hit front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife [5]." Market participants had initially treated the scandal as company-specific. That assessment shifted as the second affair became public and the board moved quickly to install interim leadership [5].Board Names Interim CEO, Analyst Reacts The board named Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a full-time successor, reported Nvidia. Kress, who has served as the company's chief financial officer since 2013, takes over at a critical juncture. Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report that the departure creates a challenging transition. "With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang, we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Luria wrote. He lowered his price target to $200 from $300 but maintained a buy rating on the stock [5]. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," added Luria [5]. The leadership change comes as Nvidia faces increasing competition in the AI chip market. The company has pursued strategic deals to maintain its dominance, including a $20 billion licensing agreement for Groq's AI technology aimed at countering Google's growing influence in inference hardware [2].Earnings Report and Analyst Outlook Nvidia recently reported quarterly results. Analysts have projected 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion. That figure is up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report that even though they expect the company to report solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term." The departure of Mr. Huang could translate to a lingering share overhang, they added [5]. The firm maintained its outperform rating on the stock. The broader context for Nvidia's report includes a market that has grown increasingly skeptical of the artificial intelligence trade. Industry projections suggest AI-related infrastructure spending could exceed $5 trillion by 2030, with data center capacity demand reaching 100 gigawatts, according to estimates cited in industry reports [3]. Whether Nvidia can meet those expectations amid leadership uncertainty remains an open question.Conclusion: Pressure on Interim CEO as Nvidia Moves Forward Kress faces immediate pressure as interim CEO after the earnings report, according to analysts. The company must demonstrate operational continuity while addressing investor concerns about strategy and succession. Oppenheimer's assessment that the departure could translate to a lingering share overhang suggests the market may need more than one earnings beat to regain confidence. The stock's longer-term direction will depend on company performance and market conditions, officials and analysts indicated. That position, combined with demand for its Blackwell platform, provides a fundamental case for the company even as leadership questions persist. The broader AI trade has shown signs of strain. Sometimes even being good at your job will not save you from unemployment. Job security can be a difficult thing to come by these days, and it seems like the folks who have it still wind up getting surprised. It's a tough job market out there. Progressive Policy reports that "U.S. layoffs are up for four consecutive years." It seems like jobs are dwindling, and you never know if you're about to be on the business end of a layoff. Employees are classically told that good performers will find their way through it, but that's not always the case. There are plenty of people who are qualified and good at their jobs who still find themselves scrambling for work. It can seem like the best course of action to try to hang onto a job for all that it's worth, but that still doesn't guarantee anything. The worker in this story was realizing that and wanted to vent some frustrations. The way they saw it, they were incredibly valuable to their workplace. The way their bosses saw it, they needed to cut costs, and they needed a quick way to do so. That can mean losing out on good labor and faithful employees.  Individual pictured is a model used for illustrative purposes. A frustrated businessman puts his head in his hands Once upon a time, loyalty was one of the most rewarded traits in an employee. If you stuck around, your company made sure you were set up for life. That doesn't seem to be the case these days. At least it wasn't in this story. This employee planned to be loyal and to continue giving good service to their employers. But their employers deeply undervalued that contribution and kicked them to the curb. It's not easy to find a new job these days, and it can feel discouraging that the people who are supposed to champion your work end up turning their back on you. That's what this employee was in the throes of navigating, and they wanted some input on the situation. When it comes to workplace issues, it's always a good idea to get some second opinions. We all have different experiences and different expertise, and it's helpful to hear what others have to say. So commenters weighed in with their advice and opinions. Two heads are almost always better than one, and that's what the internet is good for. Keep reading for more of the story and read what commenters had to say. Conflict in the Middle East has been escalating. These stories provide context for current developments and the history that led up to them. By          Jane Arraf       ,          Jawad Rizkallah                        A destroyed home in the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah in southern Lebanon. The family says Israeli forces demolished their home and two other homes of extended family when they occupied the village after a U.S.-brokered ceasefire.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon. He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home. Now there are four. A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway. Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.                  Soumaya Yaghi stands in her damaged home. Israeli forces occupied the house while they were in the village and it was set on fire as they left. The second floor was burned almost completely.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital. "This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."                  Soumaya Yaghi holds an image of her son Adel, a volunteer ambulance driver who was killed in an Israeli airstrike in March along with four other paramedics as they were burying an elderly man who had died in hospital.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  He says he warned his son that Israel could not be trusted not to kill medical personnel. "He would not listen to me. He said, 'Dad there are wounded children — we have to go rescue them,'" he says. Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff in the past two years. Asked about this airstrike, the Israeli military replied, without providing proof, that militants routinely pose as paramedics and transport weapons in ambulances for the militant group Hezbollah and its allies. It did not respond to follow-up questions pointing out the five were not killed in an ambulance but at a burial.                  A family goes through the rubble of their home after it was demolished by Israeli forces when they occupied the village. They have brought in a bulldozer to clear the rubble.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  The Kadouh family returned to the village in July when it became the first and until now only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli forces to withdraw and the Lebanese army to take over. The plan is aimed at keeping Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area, after they started firing rockets across the nearby border in solidarity with the Palestinian militant group Hamas who launched a surprise attack on southern Israel in October 2023.                  Packaging in Hebrew left behind after Israeli soldiers occupied the Kadouhs' home before the house was set on fire as Israeli forces withdrew.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  Israel responded with devastating air strikes and eventually a ground invasion, and says it has continued attacks in south Lebanon following a U.S.-brokered ceasefire this year to eliminate what it believes are continued threats to northern Israel. Israel's defense minister has acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across the Lebanese border in a self-declared security zone. When Kadouh and Yaghi returned to the village, they found that Israeli soldiers had occupied their house. And then it had been set on fire.                  Atef Kadouh sits in the middle of his burned and damaged house in south Lebanon after Israeli forces occupied the house and then withdrew in a plan to hand over security to Lebanese forces.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  Upstairs in the hallway, near scorched walls and shattered windows, what appeared to be a work roster was written on the wall in blue marker in Hebrew with the first names of Israeli soldiers. Almost everything in the house had been destroyed. Appliances — the fridge, freezer and washing machine — had bullet holes in them. Some, along with furniture, had been pushed over the second floor balcony, smashing on the ground below. Kadouh says they knew from satellite photos there was destruction in their village "but the level of destruction — we were not expecting that. Everything that could be broken they broke." In the kitchen were shattered floor tiles and kitchen cupboards wrenched from the walls. The fire appeared to be set as the soldiers were leaving. Blackened, burned food packets — fruit boxes and cans of energy drinks with Hebrew writing — were on the floor along with rotting sandwiches. In their 18-month-old grandson's bedroom, soot from a scorched ceiling dripped down on walls decorated with images of hot-air balloons and teddy bears climbing ladders to the moon. Yaghi shows a bullet — one of many she says she found throughout the house. The spent engine casing of a missile or a drone with English markings reading "propulsion unit – tactical" was found in one of the rooms.                  Soumaya Yaghi holds the metal casing of a drone or missile with English-language markings found in their home along with bullets throughout the house.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  There is no running water or electricity — Kadouh says the Israeli military destroyed the solar panels. The Lebanese army told them that when it reentered the village many of the houses had been rigged to be blown up. It said it dismantled explosives left by Israeli forces in their house and others.                  A man walks through the rubble of his destroyed home in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, Lebanon.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  The Israeli army did not reply to NPR queries about why the house was damaged or set on fire. It said military policy bars burning homes or leaving explosives. Unable to enter the village while Israeli forces were there, Kadouh said he saw a tank in their courtyard from drone images posted on social media.                  Smoke rises from an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Tebnit, Lebanon.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  Yaghi says the Israeli army used a bulldozer to uproot the trees — including the pine trees which yield one of their most prized cash crops: pine nuts. When they had killed the trees, she says they demolished the family's garage and destroyed their tractor. "We are back to square one," Kadouh says. "Starting from scratch." Even more precarious, though, than when they started decades ago. Despite a ceasefire, smoke rises from a nearby village where Israel is still attacking. Amid all the damage, the destruction of the family's trees cuts the deepest. "I tended to them as if they were small children — they were all dear to me," Kadouh says. Yaghi points out where there were fruit-bearing cactus, olive trees, a fig tree one of her sons brought from Italy, avocado trees and fields of thyme, avocado. Up until a decade ago, almost everyone here grew tobacco, diversifying crops when that market collapsed. "We raised our children through hard work and thank God all of them were educated," Yaghi says, noting with pride that they all became professionals. She maintains a visceral connection to the land. "Record this," she asks, walking next to rose bushes that have begun to bloom again. "Our land is a paradise with everything in it. Our life is this land. Our life is our homes. Even if we were to die in our homes it would be much better than to live outside."                  A man walks past a damaged mosque in the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, Lebanon. There was still no electricity or running water in the village after attacks on the infrastructure.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  Villagers here feel abandoned by even their own government — and still in danger from nearby Israeli forces. "Our homes were destroyed and no one came to check on us," Kadouh says. "Not the Lebanese state or outsiders or the parties," he says, referring to Hezbollah and its allies. "They just say 'Go back, go back' to the village. We came back and there are no essentials — no electricity, no water." Kadouh has a son in the Lebanese army and another in national security services but he says, because the Lebanese army is deliberately underequipped to avoid presenting a threat to Israel, they have never been allowed to do their jobs. "The Lebanese state never sent a soldier here to protect us," he says." That is why the parties and others came in — Hezbollah or Amal or even the Palestinian factions decades ago. "But the vacuum that the Lebanese state has left brought us to this tragedy" he says. "We love the Lebanese army — let them bring us an army, but let them protect us," he says. "This army has a rifle — Israel has an F-35" fighter jet.                  From the Lebanese Army checkpoint at the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, Lebanon, smoke is seen rising from an Israeli airstrike on a nearby town.                                                           Mohammed Yassine for NPR                                       hide caption  "But we would rather sit in the dirt," he says. "Our soul, our life is here, I was born here." Kadouh says maybe someday there will be peace with Israel, but after all the deaths and destruction, not in his lifetime — and not with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "Netanyahu is the one who killed my son. Let him bring back my son," he says. "If just yesterday Israel killed my son, am I supposed to tell the Israelis, 'Put your hand in my hand'? If they want to be our neighbors they should do good. Instead they burn us." NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Miscellaneous Articles Information on Nespresso's Project Olympus. The article is about Nespresso’s internal project to basically reduce the amount of grams per capsule that they produce. In August of 2026, I was informed by a Nespresso internal employee about “Project Olympus”. At first I didn’t think much of it and wasn’t sure how to deal with the information. It seems based on the docs that they were possibly improving the formulas, but I still questioned how that is possible with a reduction of grams of coffee. The below text is the actual Project Olympus internal text for everyone’s reference to review: PROJECT OLYMPUS: VERTUOAs part of our ongoing commitment to delivering an exceptional coffee experience, Nespresso is continuously innovating across every step of our process-while preserving the taste, quality, and consistency our consumers expect. What’s changing? Beginning in 2026, select Nespresso Vertuo coffee recipes will undergo a recipe optimization. Through advancements in grinding and roasting techniques, we’ve refined these recipes to achieve the same great taste and in-cup experience—using slightly less coffee per capsule. This change will be rolled out gradually from Q1 through Q3 2026. What’s staying the same? While the capsule weight may be slightly reduced, the core elements of the coffee experience are unchanged: These updates have been carefully validated from a sensory perspective to ensure no compromise in flavor or satisfaction. Why are we optimizing recipes? Innovation is at the heart of Nespresso. Our development teams are constantly exploring ways to improve how we roast and grind our coffees-while delivering the same consistent, high-quality results in every cup. Project Olympus reflects this effort: a behind-the-scenes optimization designed to maintain excellence, even as we evolve our processes. What if consumers ask questions? In some cases, consumers may notice that certain capsules feel lighter than before or ask about possible changes. If inquiries arise, teams should emphasize: WAVE 1: Projected transition in market Q1 2026 WAVE 2: Projected transition in market TBA Review attached memo and FAQ for additional information. No action is required as of right now. On/about Sepetember 5, 2026, I noticed a post on r/nespresso asking about whether Nespresso had changed their recipes: I then decided to offically be the first whistle blower about Project Olympus. A large number of Nespresso consumers were definitely not happy with Nespresso’s decision to reduce the number of grams per capsule. There are many users that are seriously considering to drop Nespresso and move to alternative coffee options. There are a number of people that have asked which coffees are affected, and that’s a resonable question. From what is currently being observed, almost all the range of coffees are being reduced. The only ones that don’t appear to be affected are Lungos for OL, and Alto XLs (and other larger coffees) for Vertuo. In 1971, Toyota put out an ad for the Land Cruiser. The picture was of a 12-year-old FJ25, and the headline read, "We'll know how long it lasts when the first one wears out." In the ad Toyota touts how the Land Cruiser is designed and built to last. From its steel bumper to its heavy-duty suspension to the straight-six 155-horsepower engine, everything was engineered for durability. Even back then, the Land Cruiser was already establishing a reputation for being hard to kill. Indestructible, some might even say. Earning this title was no accident. Toyota built it from tough stock — the Land Cruiser literally used commercial-grade parts the first go-around. Once it was released into the wild, it was soon being used around the world in all sorts of harsh conditions, completing jobs that tested its mettle. Land Cruisers became known as being reliable and tough.  So where did that legacy for toughness begin? Let's look at the very first step in the Land Cruiser lineage, a prototype for the Japanese National Police Reserve. Back in 1950, Toyota needed a Jeep-sized ¼-ton four-wheel-drive vehicle built with parts local to Japan. Toyota used the chassis from the one-ton SB truck, which came with a ladder-style frame, solid front and rear axles, and leaf springs. The Type B engine came from the four-ton BM truck. Let's do some quick math here–a one-ton chassis plus a four-ton engine divided by a ¼-ton truck equals a chassis that was overkill and an engine that was understressed. Thankfully, that turned out to be a great equation and became the template for Land Cruisers to come. To see how that reputation evolved, let's next take a look at the legendary Land Cruiser 40 Series, which included the iconic FJ40. Launched in 1960, the FJ40 rode on a heavy-duty ladder-style frame to tackle high-stress and twisting forces. This was the second generation powered by the F-series engine, an inline-6 with a cast-iron block. It was built to have high torque at low rpms, keeping it understressed and reliable. That engine, incidentally, was in production 43 years before being retired, which meant it had the longest run of any Toyota engine. It became known worldwide as a reliable, durable all-terrain vehicle over its 24-year production run.  Toyota engineered the Land Cruiser to be tougher than its environment. The chassis and suspension were overbuilt for the vehicle, and the engine was designed to keep on going. Travel to just about any remote part of the planet, and you will still see a Land Cruiser variant being put to work. Land Cruisers have been used worldwide as farm trucks, fire trucks, and even combat platforms. They also deliver mail in the Outback in Australia, save lives as ambulances in Costa Rica, and are the vehicle of choice for aid organizations and the United Nations and the Red Cross. Land Cruisers are trusted around the world to handle these tough tasks for one reason — they consistently get the job done.  That ethos was passed down through the generation of trucks that followed. Yes, they got more comfortable, but they didn't compromise on the core promise. The understressed (and still thirsty) engines changed over the years, but the stout cast-iron block stuck around in the North American market until the 200-series arrival in 2008. The frame got boxed in 1967 and body-on-frame construction is still in place today. Solid front axles were standard until 1998 with the 100-series. Throughout these measured changes over the Land Cruiser's 75-year history, there has been one other constant — the passion of Land Cruiser owners. These enthusiasts have arguably done more to contribute to building the reputation than anything else. Ask any Land Cruiser owner about their truck, and will gladly tell you how 200,000 miles is just getting broken in. As an owner of two — one at 240,000 miles and another at 284,000 miles — I can confirm. Claims of 400,000 and 500,000 miles are not unheard. This trust in their vehicles and reluctance to part with them is a good part of why Land Cruisers have such good resale value. Those looking to get into a new Land Cruiser are in luck. In 2024, after a two-year absence, Toyota gave us the revival of the off-road icon in the form of a brand-new Land Cruiser. It comes from the Prado line of Land Cruiser, which has been upholding the Land Cruiser name and reputation worldwide since 1990. Will it be another legend?  Time will tell.

You’re using the new Bored Panda. Send feedback If a toy doesn’t do something as basic as entertain a child, then what’s its real purpose? Well, I am no expert in the matter. That’s why Bored Panda got in touch with product designer Sharanya Salehittal for an interview. She has some experience designing kids’ toys, so she shared her insights with us.  She first spoke about the importance of toys for kids. Beyond making them happy, she stressed how they support brain development. She believes toys also boost children’s imagination and spark their creativity. That’s why she says it’s important to consider all these nuances when designing toys.  We asked our expert to elaborate on what to consider when designing toys for kids. She first discussed safety, ensuring every toy meets strict regulations and avoiding small parts or toxic materials that could harm children. Next, the focus should be on the ergonomics for comfort and ease of use.  How a child’s hands, eyes, and imagination will interact with the toy is pretty important, she continued. Also, the bright colors, different shapes, and engaging textures aren’t just for show; they help grab a kid’s attention and ignite their imagination. Sharanya narrated, “Toys play a big role in how kids develop physically, mentally, and socially. A well-designed toy can help a child learn to grasp objects, solve problems, or even express emotions. For instance, something like LEGO can help teach kids spatial reasoning and patience. Designers aim to create toys that challenge kids just enough to build confidence, without overwhelming them.” Our expert noted that designers also consider the emotional connection a child can have with a toy. We often see little ones cradling stuffed animals and taking them everywhere they go, and that in itself is a sign of a good toy. She believes that when kids form this connection, it can have a lasting impact, making playtime more meaningful and memorable.  Sharanya also explained that to understand better how a child’s mind works, designers sometimes work with child psychologists. This gives them perspective on how to make a toy more intuitive and inviting. After all, kids should not be frustrated while using it; rather, it should be a seamless experience that lets them enjoy it. Never miss a story that brings joy to the world.Add us on Google Another important point Sharanya made was sustainability. Whether it’s recycled plastics, biodegradable fabrics, or sustainably sourced wood, she said many designers are turning to eco-friendly materials. The focus is also on durability, so toys can be passed on or resold instead of being thrown away. In fact, research shows that the global sustainable toys market is poised for substantial growth, expanding from $16,651 million in 2021 to an anticipated $66,155.5 million by 2033.  It also reveals that this expansion is driven primarily by a significant shift in consumer behavior. Modern parents are increasingly prioritizing eco-friendly, non-toxic, and educational products for their children, supported by government promotion. Lastly, we asked our expert to speak about what makes a toy “bad” or “weird.” She said that such toys fail in more than one key area.  “It might be too complicated, with vague instructions or too many buttons that overwhelm a child. Others lack clear purpose, leaving kids unsure what to do with them. Poor aesthetics, like dull colors or awkward shapes, can also make a toy unappealing. And, of course, safety oversights, like sharp edges or choking hazards, can turn playtime into a risk,” she summed up. Something not working? Tell us. It helps us improve the new Bored Panda.
