Though James Bond creator Ian Fleming's influence is still acutely felt with the long-running movie series adapting his literary character, the films have taken considerable creative liberties for decades. Adaptations of Fleming's work had grown significantly looser as early as the Sean Connery era, while many of the movies named after them still contained elements from the stories. A prime example is, despite "The Spy Who Loved Me" being plagued by copyright troubles, it still retained a villain with metal-capped teeth. But by the end of Roger Moore's lengthy tenure, the movies had largely ditched incorporating any of Fleming's elements, though that wasn't true of 2006's "Casino Royale." We're taking a look back at the James Bond movies that are not based on Ian Fleming's books and short stories. Some of the entries here take their titles from short stories written by Ian Fleming but, frankly, nothing else. Outside of the inclusion of Bond and his usual allies and enemies, these cinematic narratives really strike out on their own creatively.  Here are all 10 James Bond movies not based on Ian Fleming's books ranked, going in their own direction with the super-spy. Pierce Brosnan currently remains the only actor whose entire run as James Bond featured original narratives for his movies, rather than drawing directly from a specific Fleming story. In taking Bond out of the Cold War setting in which he originated, this led to an uneven tenure, despite Brosnan's best efforts. However, nothing could quite save Brosnan's last turn as 007 in 2002's "Die Another Day," opening with a title track by Madonna that sounded dated when it was released. The movie has Bond square off with a rogue North Korean general while trying to identify who betrayed him on a mission that led to a prolonged torturous imprisonment. IMDb names "Die Another Day" as the worst James Bond movie, a dubious distinction that is, unfortunately, well-deserved. The movie opens with Bond infiltrating North Korea by surfing, because that's clearly what the kids are still into, and it only gets worse from there. This backslide into mediocrity spreads to the cinematography, complete with shoddy CG effects and random slow-motion sequences for no discernible reason other than an attempt to look cool. An absolute travesty and an embarrassing way for Brosnan to end his time as Bond, "Die Another Day" is a grating viewing experience. Yes, "A View to a Kill," Moore's swan song to the franchise, takes its title from the 1960 Fleming short story "From a View to a Kill." But whereas the literary namesake features Bond hunting a motorcycle-driving assassin in France, the 1985 movie pits 007 against an immoral tech tycoon before it was cool. The tycoon in question is Max Zorin (Christopher Walken), a sadistic figure looking to corner the microchip market by destroying Silicon Valley. But outside of Walken chewing the scenery, joined by Grace Jones playing his enforcer, and a memorable title track by Duran Duran, the movie falls flat. Roger Moore was horrified by "A View to a Kill," particularly the widespread casual violence, as Zorin mercilessly murders many of his associates. We're personally horrified by how rough around the edges the overall movie is, from its lackluster stunts to its abrupt finale. To make matters worse, when the movie's filming wrapped, at 57 years old, Moore looks visibly aged out of playing a spry secret agent. A half-hearted end to Moore's celebrated run playing James Bond, "A View to a Kill" feels as tired as its lead actor. Daniel Craig's sophomore outing as Bond in 2008's "Quantum of Solace" also takes its title from a 1960 short story written by Fleming. But the literary tale simply follows Bond as he attends a dinner party in Nassau where he hears a story about an unhappy marriage. With that certainly not enough for an action movie to go off of, the film instead functions as a direct sequel to "Casino Royale," opening minutes later. Bond uncovers a global network that's infiltrated government organizations worldwide, including MI6, while contending with his own unresolved grief over his recently deceased lover Vesper Lynd (Eva Green). For as much grief as "Quantum of Solace" gets, constantly existing in the shadow of "Casino Royale," it's a perfectly watchable Bond movie. The shortest in the series to date, the film does feel like a parade of action set pieces, but Craig's performance grounds the spectacle. The movie's themes about water scarcity and a cabal of affluent influencers trying to manipulate international governments does feel prescient. Coming off as an extended epilogue to "Casino Royale" rather than its own standalone experience, "Quantum of Solace" really works best watched in concert with its immediate predecessor. Compared to its more action-oriented predecessor, "The World Is Not Enough" tried to lean more into dramatic territory. The 1999 movie opens with Bond (Brosnan) tricked into delivering a bomb to MI6 related to a kidnapping plot involving oil heiress Elektra King (Sophie Marceau). After being assigned to protect Elektra, Bond hunts down the terrorist responsible for the explosive incident, only to uncover a whole plot targeting vital oil pipelines into Europe. This leads Bond to realize that Elektra is not as helpless or innocent as he believed when they struck up their illicit romance. Taking its title from Bond's family motto introduced in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service," "The World Is Not Enough" tries to feel like a more personal adventure for 007 accordingly. But as good a femme fatale as Sophie Marceau is, the movie never quite delivers on the emotional potential that it aspires to. The action is a bit lackluster too, feeling like something more akin to a theme park stunt spectacular than a blockbuster set piece. Underscoring that Brosnan was often working with lesser material during his Bond run, "The World Is Not Enough" couldn't live up to its creative ambitions. There was a lot of expectation riding on "Spectre" after the critical and commercial success of its immediate predecessor "Skyfall." The movie also marks the first official Bond movie since "Diamonds Are Forever" to explicitly include Ernst Stavro Blofeld, after protracted legal issues prevented the villain's usage. This time, Blofeld is played by Christoph Waltz, with the added backstory that he and Bond grew up together contentiously as surrogate brothers, before the criminal mastermind faked his death. Since then, the movie reveals Blofeld has secretly been tormenting Bond from the shadows, leading to their eventual unhappy reunion for the fate of the world. "Spectre" falls into the trap of trying to emulate "Skyfall" too much, right down to directly lifting music tracks from the preceding movie's score. The idea of Blofeld being Bond's brother figure, a concept also introduced in the 007 spoof "Austin Powers in Goldmember," is a laughable way to make their dynamic feel more personal. What salvages the movie from its lackluster script is its top-notch cinematography by Hoyte van Hoytema, particularly its stunning opening scene in Mexico City. Brosnan's sophomore outing as Bond in 1997's "Tomorrow Never Dies" doesn't get as much credit as it deserves, overshadowed by its more successful predecessor. Another prescient entry in the series as far as its story is concerned, the main villain is a murderous media mogul providing his own news output. In order to take his media empire to the next level, Elliot Carver (Jonathan Pryce) tries to orchestrate a war between the United Kingdom and China. Bond and Chinese intelligence operative Wai Lin (Michelle Yeoh) work together to expose Carver's plot and prevent the conflict from breaking out. Considering "Tomorrow Never Dies" scrapped its script days before filming, it's a wonder the movie came out as well as it did. The movie goes even more global than many other series' entries, taking Bond everywhere from Carver's offices in Germany to the streets of Saigon. What holds the movie back is that its plot does feel visibly rushed, while none of the action set pieces are as satisfying as the big moments in "GoldenEye." A glossier approach to the franchise than its predecessor's post-Cold War grittiness, "Tomorrow Never Dies" is a serviceable entry in Brosnan's Bond legacy. When Daniel Craig closed out his celebrated run as James Bond, he did so with a bang, leaving no stone unturned. This made "No Time to Die" the longest James Bond movie ever, opening with Bond believing his latest serious paramour, Madeleine Swann (Léa Seydoux), had betrayed him to Spectre. After abruptly leaving the service in the wake of this assumption, Bond is pulled back into action when a secret weapon is stolen from the British government. In the process of destroying this deadly project, Bond has to face familiar faces from his life before a fatal showdown against the terrorist Lyutsifer Safin (Rami Malek). While it could've trimmed about 15 minutes from its runtime, "No Time to Die" provides Craig with a largely solid farewell. From the dusty streets of Italy where Bond tries to get closure for the events of "Casino Royale" to its explosive finale, the movie hits all the right notes. The film's villains, including Malek's Safin, are a bit of a mixed bag, but the action, including a centerpiece sequence in Cuba, is competently staged. A satisfying end to Craig's five-movie run as 007, "No Time to Die" sticks the landing even if it takes some time to get there. While it's not as fondly remembered today, 1989's "License to Kill" is an essential James Bond everyone should see at least once. Timothy Dalton's second and final turn as 007, the movie begins with Felix Leiter (David Hedison) and his new bride being attacked by drug lord Franz Sanchez (Robert Davi). With MI6 refusing to retaliate, considering the incident an outside matter, Bond angrily resigns from the service and sets out to avenge his friend. This unsanctioned vendetta eventually reveals that there is more at stake with Sanchez's latest scheme than Bond realized. Though Dalton brought a more serious edge to Bond with his first movie in the role, "The Living Daylights," "License to Kill" is where he really cuts loose. Long before Daniel Craig did it, Dalton played Bond as a mean, lethal type that had no problem with getting his hands dirty to get the job done. These harder-edged sensibilities caught people off-guard, with the memory of the light-hearted Roger Moore tenure still fresh in their minds. But if you're looking to see why Timothy Dalton is filmmaker Christopher Nolan's favorite Bond actor, "License to Kill" is the perfect showcase. After a six-year hiatus following "License to Kill," James Bond finally returned to the silver screen in 1995, this time with Pierce Brosnan playing the role. "GoldenEye" was almost the end of the James Bond franchise as it tried to find its way after the Cold War. The specter of those global tensions certainly inform the movie's story, with Bond learning a Soviet-era weapons satellite has been hijacked. Venturing into the heart of Russia to identify the culprit, Bond comes face-to-face with his old friend and former 00 Agent Alec Trevelyan (Sean Bean), now leading a crime syndicate. The Bond movie series needed a shot of adrenaline if it hoped to stay alive after the Cold War, and "GoldenEye" delivered. Brosnan strikes the perfect balance between Moore's self-aware charm and Dalton's steely-eyed intensity while exploring the nuances of the character like never before. The action is as memorable as the franchise gets, and the supporting cast around Brosnan all turn in fantastic work, especially Bean as Trevelyan. Cementing the franchise's relevance beyond a set time period, "GoldenEye" remains the most important box office hit in Bond history, and that comes from a film of enduring quality. Speaking of box office success, "Skyfall" became the biggest James Bond movie ever when it opened in theaters in 2012. Continuing Daniel Craig's run after a four-year hiatus, the movie has Bond reconcile with his lethal occupation's toll on his body and mind after a disastrous mission in Istanbul. Returning to duty after London is attacked by a shadowy figure linked to M (Judi Dench) and her own unresolved legacy, Bond has to contend with his own advancing age. Fortunately, this mission and its eccentric villain Raoul Silva (Javier Bardem) are just the things to help Bond overcome his midlife crisis. Released in time for the film series' 50th anniversary, "Skyfall" feels like a celebration and commentary on the legacy of James Bond. Under sharp direction from Sam Mendes, the movie beautifully illustrates those themes while delivering bombastic action sequences, including a fantastic fight scene in Shanghai. Elevating the proceedings is haunting cinematography from Roger Deakins, really accentuating the light and shadows that Bond frequently plays in. An absolute masterpiece from top to bottom, "Skyfall" deconstructs Bond and thematically rebuilds him for the 21st century.

From Micheltorena Street, the Baldwin Residence looks like a low roof behind a hedge, with a ribbon of windows tucked under the eaves. From downhill, the same house seems to hang in the treetops. The difference gets at the problem John Lautner had to solve in 1955: how to build a three-bedroom home on a steep lot in Los Angeles’s Silver Lake neighborhood and give the people inside a sweeping view without putting their whole lives on display. Lautner designed the 1,679-square-foot home for Rosemary and Joseph Baldwin. Joseph was a commercial artist, so the plan had to make room for his work as well as ordinary domestic life. The house came onto the market for the first time in 71 years in October 2026 and sold on November 18 for $2.6 million, about half a million above asking. The sale brought fresh attention to a house that’s easy to miss from the street. Designer: John Lautner        Lautner gave the two main parts of the house different relationships to the slope. The bedroom wing follows the hillside, while the wedge-shaped living room projects out over it. A winding driveway descends to a carport tucked underneath. Slender posts and shear walls support the house, leaving the drop visible beneath the living room and its wraparound teak deck. I like that you can still see the ground falling away. That gap does as much to explain the house as any aerial photograph of its angular roof. Inside the living room, tall panes meet at an angle, with no bulky corner post to interrupt the view where they join. The room gives you reasons to look inward, too. The ceiling folds down like an upside-down pyramid, and small triangular windows bring in light above eye level. In Cameron Carothers’s photographs, a sofa sits beside the brick fireplace. That’s where I’d put it, too. The brick gives the seating area a definite edge, so the whole room doesn’t have to be arranged like an audience facing the glass.         On the other side of the fireplace, Lautner set aside a studio for Joseph with light from the north. It’s a small distinction that matters: the space to work belongs to the house without taking over the living room. The bedrooms get a separate hallway with a parquet floor, and each still has its original built-ins. In rooms this compact, putting storage into the architecture means one less bulky piece of furniture to find a place for. The showier angles get the photographs; I suspect those built-ins would earn their keep every morning. The kitchen meets the outdoors at a much more ordinary scale. Terrazzo runs from the skylit entry through the kitchen and out to the sculpture garden, where exposed joists extend overhead to form a pergola. From the little dining table beside the sliding glass door, the view is a tree, a low wall, and a few sculptures. Even with the door closed in the photograph, the continuation of the floor makes the garden feel like part of the place where you’d eat breakfast. No panorama necessary.    I’m glad the original laminate counters are still there, along with the wood cabinets and open shelves. The kitchen is modest in size, which might matter more on a weeknight with two people trying to cook than it does in a photograph. Still, I’d be slower to change it than the square footage alone might suggest. The table has a good spot, and making the kitchen bigger wouldn’t necessarily make that spot any better. Even the smaller bathroom gets its own version of the view. In the photographs, daylight catches the angled ceiling, and a high window frames a patch of blue. Nobody needs the San Gabriel Mountains as a backdrop to brushing their teeth. Lautner knew when a little sky would do.    Every craft that works in color figured this out long ago. How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing?  The Open Social Web Alliance aims to provide the answers.  A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email. Whether your address is hosted by Proton, Posteo, Gmail or GMX, your digital letters reach their destination. This is the idea we build on. The year is 2028. Thanks to smart investment and political foresight, the Open Social Web has achieved its breakthrough. More than 100 million people connect, communicate and experience the world of open social networks. No platform economy à la Meta, ByteDance, Alphabet and co., no stressful digital moves and no toxic design. It works just like email: whether on Mastodon, Eurosky’s Mu or Streamplace, you have one account, your own posts and content, your own choices, and the freedom to connect with 100 million users worldwide. A critical mass of users in Europe has turned its back on the platform monopolies and created a free market built on interoperable infrastructure. Today, users decide for themselves which content, which algorithms and which applications they want to use. Closed platforms have become open networks. On the ActivityPub and AT Protocol protocols (as well as Matrix for direct messaging), an ecosystem of non-commercial, public service and commercial offerings has emerged. They enrich and complement public-interest projects such as Mastodon and Eurosky, and they communicate with one another through shared interfaces. This vision describes the Open Social Web (OSW): a decentralised, public-interest infrastructure for digital communication, based on open standards and interoperable protocols. The idea of an Open Social Web is not new. The Fediverse has been in development since 2008 and is home to diverse, vibrant communities that build individual applications and run instances. While its focus has so far been on Europe, North America and Japan, there are now more than 100 applications, such as Mastodon, Loops and PeerTube, and more than 42,000 active instances worldwide. Even so, the number of active users, around 13 million, is growing only slowly. The ATmosphere community has been developing since 2022, primarily in North America but increasingly in Europe and beyond. It currently has around 43 million registered accounts and dozens of implementations and applications, such as Eurosky’s Mu, Gander and Sill. For many reasons, both protocol-based social networks are attractive alternatives to the platform economy dominated by Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet. So why have people been so hesitant to switch? We have identified five key challenges: infrastructure, governance, funding, appeal and public mandate. Below, we set out how we can overcome them and make the Open Social Web Alliance a shared success. An ecosystem like this does not emerge on its own. Our roadmap shows how the Open Social Web could reach a relevant scale within just a few months. It takes political will, smart regulation, sufficient funding and a broad coalition of actors willing to share responsibility. The task is big. But the levers are there.  As a first step, we are founding the Open Social Web Alliance: an open alliance of stakeholders from civil society, research, business, media, culture and the public sector who are committed to the shared governance of the OSW. It brings together a wide range of existing communities and initiatives and is to be supported in future by a publicly funded secretariat. Its central goal: building and operating the OSW’s core infrastructure (see Section 2.1, Infrastructure).  Our roadmap envisions that the German federal government will explicitly support the Alliance, for instance by acting as patron of an Open Social Web Summit in autumn 2026, to which everyone with an interest in the OSW would be invited. At the summit, the Alliance would adopt its charter, setting out how it admits new members and how it intends to implement its governance going forward (see Section 2.2, Governance). By spring 2027, public funding for the infrastructure would be in place, along with a first core funding round of public and private capital for innovation and applications (see Section 2.3, Funding). The Alliance would publish its first Social Web Health Report, featuring findings from user surveys, legal, technical and academic analyses, and clear recommendations for further development (see Section 2.4, Appeal). In parallel, the federal and state governments would ensure that the legal basis for cooperation between public service media, other media, business and civil society is established (see Section 2.5, Public Mandate). The federal government would also champion the OSW idea at EU level, for instance through an implementation push for effective digital legislation. As key stakeholders such as the federal government adopt OSW applications as their primary channel of communication, influential creators and publishers would follow suit, and central political debates would quickly shift to the Open Social Web. Taken together, these measures would reduce the influence and appeal of today’s dominant Big Tech platforms. The Open Social Web Alliance is looking for allies: people and organisations who are convinced that genuine social networks can create real value.  We look forward to hearing from you. Rob LeFebvre is an editor and writer focusing on consumer and enterprise technologies for a broad range of outlets. He’s been writing online for more than 15 years; before that he was a special educator for kids with severe disabilities. Rob has been an Editorial Director at Lifewire, a news writer at Engadget, and a senior contributor at Cult of Mac. He's written about PCs, Macs, mobile phones, and games, created newsrooms from the ground up, and has extensive experience reviewing hardware, software, and games across his career.   I just finished Monsters of Ohio, the latest novel by John Scalzi. It's amazing, fast-paced, and funny as heck, and I read the whole thing on a tiny e-ink reader. The Xteink X4 Pro handled the novel easily and, thanks to its magnetic back and mini size, was always with me, in my pocket or my EDC bag. It charges quickly on the optional charging base, and I'm loving this little thing. I think you will, too. At $99, it undercuts the base Kindle's new $149.99 price and adds the front light and touchscreen the original X4 lacked. I tested it on Xteink's stock software, which is where most buyers will start. About this review: Xteink provided MUO with the Xteink X4 Pro for review. The company had no input in this article. All views are my own. The Xteink X4 Pro is a pocket-sized e-ink eReader built for reading on the go. Its 4.3-inch, 219 PPI display adds an adjustable front light with warm and cool tones, so you can read in the dark, and it pairs a touchscreen with physical page-turn buttons. At 72 grams and under 6mm thick, it slips into a pocket or bag, and a magnetic back attaches to MagSafe and Qi2 phones. It reads DRM-free EPUB and TXT books natively, with MOBI and PDF converted through the Xteink app, and includes a 16GB microSD card expandable to 256GB. Books transfer over Wi-Fi with the app’s Cloud Sync. Charging is through pogo pins, using an included magnetic USB-C adapter or an optional charging stand. You can grab the Xteink X4 Pro from Amazon or Xteink's official website in a bundle that includes a free magnetic case, protective case, and a couple of screen protectors for $99, as long as you want the Space Black color.  The box came in the mail at about the size of a thick CD. It's all cardboard, very eco-friendly, with a QR code to help you download the app to your phone. There's a spot in there for the little proprietary pin charger, but no USB-C cable; you'll have to provide your own. The company sent me a gray unit, and tossed in one of the optional charging stands, which has a place for the little charging adapter to go in it. The box also included some adhesive magnetic stickers to fit on a non-MagSafe phone, too. The magnets themselves on the unit will let it stick to any MagSafe phone, but they're not super strong. I ended up having the eReader come off my phone in my pocket, so I stopped trying to keep them attached. Plus, my iPhone Duo's passport-style design meant that the Xteink X4 Pro stuck out from the bottom by a couple of inches. Not a deal-breaker, for sure, but a slab phone will be better suited to this form factor. I just keep it in my pocket or EDC bag, so it's always with me. Charging happens via pogo pins on the tiny magnetic adapter, which can easily fall off or not connect completely. It's also small enough that I can easily see losing it; a replacement is only $6, so not the end of the world. I'd have preferred a USB-C charging port, but this works fine. I charged this thing twice during my time with it; once when I got it, then again when it got down to 20% after a long day of reading on it. It charged up to full in about half an hour. It's tiny; Boox's new Picco is smaller, but this is the smallest eReader I've ever used. That size makes sure it's always with me; I keep it near my keys and wallet so I grab it to go out the front door. Xteink doesn't give an official battery life figure for the 1,100mAh battery, but in my time with the device, it only needed a charge after heavy reading with the light enabled. Even still, a half-hour top-up made it a non-issue. The 219 PPI text display is less sharp than on, say, a Kindle or Kobo, which use 300 PPI displays, but it's just fine at this screen size. I was able to read easily in bright and indirect light, even without the screen light this new model provides. That front light adjusts brightness and color temperature, even though it doesn't have an auto-brightness or scheduling feature. It's easy to turn on and off, though, with just a swipe from the top, which also exposes the light/dark mode display along with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth toggles. Like all e-ink displays, this one flashes a refresh every once in a while, which might be a bit more noticeable on this tiny screen. Still, it's not a problem and never interfered with my reading. The touch input is new to this X4 Pro, too. I tend to like buttons on my eReaders, anyway, so I don't rely on touch, but it was nice to have in certain hand positions. The left button turns the page backward, while the right button and side of the screen advance the page. The buttons work every time, while the touch can be less than responsive at times, requiring a second tap. Kindle, Kobo, and Nook owners have it so easy. Just pop into the store on the device, the web, or phone app, purchase the books you want, and they're sent right to the device. Same with library books via Libby; getting these on traditional eReaders is super convenient and easy. Not so with a device like the Xteink X4 Pro; you'll have to source your own DRM-free books and then send them to your device via Wi-Fi. It's not super hard, but it does add a layer of friction between you and your reading material. There are basically four ways to get your ebook onto your Xteink reader: add the books to the microSD card, and pop it back into the reader, use the Xteink phone app (this is what I did), use Calibre to wirelessly transfer books from your computer to your eReader (for those of you with extensive Calibre libraries), or grab your books from an OPDS book server catalog (this is more complex, but feels more like having a built-in book store). I bought Monsters of Ohio from ebooks.com, having filtered the list of books in the sci-fi genre to "DRM-free," then saved the download to Drive. I then used the Xteink app to import the Drive file, and synced it via Cloud Sync in the app. It was fast; the whole novel appeared in seconds. I'm not one to overly customize my screens and such, but the Xteink app has a bunch of ways to add cover images to your X4 Pro. I didn't find it super intuitive to use, though, so after figuring out how to set the "off" state to the cover of whatever I was currently reading, I gave up on it. The companion app is cluttered, to say the least. Alongside feeds, weather, and a reading schedule, it pushes extras like a lyric poster, a work badge, receipts, and book cover makers. None of it helps you read. I've considered flashing to the open-source CrossPoint firmware once it's released for the X4 Pro, as it adds better book formatting, more fonts and layout options, a dictionary, and a night mode. There is a spot to download public domain work in English, so it's not a total loss.  We want to hear from you. Stubb said late on Sunday that Finland would continue working to maintain stability and security in the Gulf of Finland and thanked the authorities for their response to Saturday’s incident. Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it was previously anchored. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship. A fire aboard the Sparta II continued to burn through the night despite efforts to extinguish it, the Finnish coastguard said. “Unfortunately, the consequences of Russia’s war of aggression are also visible in our region,” Stubb said on X. Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck. Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory. The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X. The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday. Finland’s military said last week that it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks. The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange. The vessel is subject to United States sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 joined the Nasdaq in correction territory as AI stocks plunged further, but 2026 is also winding down, and Wall Street is already putting out predictions for 2027. Analysts see solid gains ahead, with the U.S. economy expected to continue chugging along on the back of massive hyperscaler spending and resilient consumers. Some also welcomed the recent decline for taking froth off markets that might otherwise start looking overheated. Even this week’s selloff, which marked the worst weekly loss since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, was largely dismissed as a move driven more by emotion than fundamentals.  “This does not mean stampedes are uninformative or palpitations never presage heart attacks, but today’s panic does not feel like an AI bust,” Viktor Shvets, head of global desk strategy at Macquarie Capital, said in a note Friday. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager and partner at Founder ETFs, quipped that the market is “selling first and asking questions later.” And Jamie Cox, managing partner for Harris Financial Group, predicted investors will “return to rationality” and look instead to consumption-boosting GDP.  Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley chief U.S. equity strategist Michael Wilson said earlier this week that the S&P 500 would finish 2027 at 8,700, representing a 26% jump from current levels and a 15% rally when he made the call. “We see the mid-cycle transition now ending with a more stable mid-cycle backdrop evolving in 2027,” he wrote. Goldman Sachs also sees the broad market index soaring to 8,700 next year, “albeit with higher volatility than in recent years.” Peter Oppenheimer, the bank’s chief global equity strategist, said that while corporate earnings growth will slow, inflation, bond yields, and oil prices will also moderate. “We expect the equity bull market to continue.” Elsewhere, estimates were less bullish but still upbeat. UBS Global Wealth Management put the S&P 500 at 8,200 next year, implying 19% upside from Friday’s close.  Although it sees more earnings gains in 2027, Wall Street is focusing on whether the investment cycle can support profits into 2028, UBS explained. “Cannibalization, financing, and execution risks around AI have increased while expectations and index concentration remain high,” it added. “The market is therefore more sensitive to earnings disappointment or a further rise in discount rates.” Wells Fargo’s S&P 500 outlook in 2027 is also for 8,200, which assumes slower profit growth as well. But then there’s Steve Chiavarone, chief investment officer for equities at Federated Hermes, who has a year-end view of 10,000—or a 45% surge from current levels. He brushed aside this month’s midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep Congress and several state capitals. While Wall Street fears the blue tsunami will slow the AI infrastructure boom, Chiavarone said risks to the buildout are overblown. Even a slight retreat would be positive. “A modest pullback in the data center buildout could give cash flows time to catch up, easing inflation pressures and making the investment boom more sustainable,” he argued. Slower prices could prevent additional rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, which has grown more hawkish as policymakers become impatient with inflation exceeding their 2% target for over five years. Although Wall Street sees more tightening in the coming months, some analysts also anticipate rate cuts later in 2027 as inflation cools. But that assumes the Iran war will be over some time next year. For now, Gaurav Mallik, chief investment officer at Modera Wealth Management, described the market slide as a “garden variety correction,” with stock leadership rotating from tech to industrials and financials. “The pullback in stocks sets the market up nicely for 2027, which we believe will be a high-single-digit year,” he added. “Multiples are shrinking, and total returns are a function of earnings growth, which so far looks robust for 2027.” Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing. © 2026 Fortune Media IP Limited. Why announced demand is a poor guide to durable investment  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  The AI infrastructure market presents an apparent contradiction. Memory is in critically short supply. TrendForce reports that conventional DRAM contract prices increased by roughly 93% to 98% in the first quarter of 2026, as suppliers gave priority to server applications and cloud providers fought for available capacity. High-bandwidth memory shortages may persist until 2030, according to a warning from SK Hynix. Chief Technology Officer at EXANTE. At the same time, announced data center demand increasingly exceeds what can realistically be delivered. In Britain, applications for grid connections rose from 41GW to 125GW in less than a year, largely because of data center projects. One market is defined by physical scarcity. The other contains more proposed capacity than the system can accommodate. Together, they demonstrate why declared demand is a poor substitute for irreversible investment. During the 2023 memory downturn, manufacturers cut production as prices plummeted. SK Hynix alone reported an annual operating loss of 7.73 trillion won. When AI demand accelerated, suppliers entered the boom with a recent reminder of how quickly shortages can turn into gluts. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron account for around 90% of the DRAM market. They have responded to AI demand by directing more production towards high-margin server memory and HBM. This has tightened the supply of conventional memory used elsewhere, even as smaller buyers struggle to compete with hyperscalers for allocations. Memory and storage companies are still investing. Micron, for example, has outlined more than $250 billion in US manufacturing and research investment through 2035. But new capacity arrives slowly. Fabrication plants require years of construction, equipment installation and qualification. TrendForce expects most near-term supply growth to come from process improvements rather than major increases in wafer capacity. A new fab is effectively a demand forecast made in concrete. To approve one, a manufacturer must believe that today’s demand will survive several generations of chips and AI products. It must also accept that improvements in model efficiency or changing architectures could reduce the amount or type of memory required before the plant reaches volume production. The companies closest to the physical bottleneck are expanding, but in stages, and their caution sits uneasily beside the AI industry’s largest demand projections. Data center developers face different incentives. Land, power and equipment must be secured long before a facility can begin operating. When each resource is scarce, applying early and applying for more than ultimately required can appear rational. The problem emerges when those applications are added together and treated as a reliable forecast of future demand. Britain offers a clear example. Ofgem says data center projects accounted for at least 80GW of the recent increase in grid connection applications. The regulator is now proposing commitment fees and additional milestones, requiring developers to demonstrate financial and commercial readiness, including procurement activity. The reform recognizes a basic distinction: reserving capacity is not the same as building it. A project can have a site, a public announcement and a place in the grid queue without having a committed customer, completed financing or a realistic route to energization. We should not assume deception. Developers are responding to a system in which waiting can mean losing access altogether. However, the aggregate pipeline becomes misleading when every request is interpreted as independent, funded demand. Infrastructure planners should focus on how much capacity has secured power, financing, equipment and customers, and how much ultimately reaches operation. AI financing creates another difficulty when measuring the market. Chipmakers increasingly invest in companies that are also current or prospective customers. The most prominent example was Nvidia’s proposed investment of up to $100 billion in OpenAI, linked to the deployment of at least 10GW of Nvidia systems. In December 2025, Nvidia said the definitive agreement had not yet been completed and that the potential OpenAI purchases were not included in its existing chip bookings. Supplier financing is not inherently improper, as strategic investment can help new technologies reach commercial scale. But it complicates how demand should be read. When a hardware supplier invests in an AI company that then uses part of that capital to buy computing infrastructure, the same relationship generates both an investment asset and potential product revenue. Demand may still be genuine, but it is not fully independent of the company supplying it. Technology leaders assessing the market should therefore distinguish between revenue funded by end customers and demand supported by capital circulating within the AI supply chain. These two indicators provide different evidence about whether infrastructure will remain economically productive. CIOs, cloud providers and enterprises planning AI capacity should remember that a real memory shortage can coexist with speculative data center pipelines. Scarcity today does not prove that every projected workload will materialize, just as abandoned projects do not make the current shortage imaginary. The most useful indicators are the commitments that are expensive to reverse: binding customer contracts, non-refundable deposits, secured power, equipment already procured and facilities that have entered construction. Once a data center becomes operational, utilization and revenue from external customers provide stronger evidence than its announced capacity. Infrastructure plans should follow the same logic. Capacity can be added in stages as workloads, utilization and returns become measurable. Long-term commitments should be matched to demand that has already demonstrated some durability. The defining contradiction of the AI boom is that the industry is over-ordering and under-building at the same time. The businesses taking the longest-term physical risk appear less certain than the headline numbers imply. For anyone making infrastructure decisions, that gap may be the most revealing evidence in the market. We've featured the best AI tool. And nobody learns from past mistakes   Every time I read about another company laying off managers and ‘running flatter’, I think about how absurd it is. I can’t understand why senior leaders don’t see the harm they inflict on their own companies.   It’s also quite personal, of course.   So I decided to speak with someone who’s been through more of these cycles than I have. I’ve been enjoying Suzan’s newsletter for years - she’s an organizational development consultant who works with tech leaders. After reading her article about being laid off 6(!) times before becoming a COO, I knew we had to talk.   Today we’ll cover:   Why the EM role specifically is under attack   Repeating history - Google and Microsoft already ran this experiment   How flattening impacts the company   What EMs can do about it   Mic to Suzan!   There is this common idea that with AI, we can run much leaner and that agents can replace much of the human work.    The first attack was on software engineers: for a short while, leaders claimed that the profession was dead. That turned around pretty quickly, with companies understanding they still need experienced engineers to decide what to build, review what LLMs produce, and maintain the systems afterward. Engineers now make up 55% of Big Tech hiring, up from 46% in 2019.   But with managers, it’s harder to justify, and we are repeating the flattening cycle that we went through 10 years ago. Some of the bigger tech companies started by laying off middle managers, and the smaller companies started to think, “Oh, I should consider that too” (whether their own conditions are the same or not).    And when leaders look at the first-line Engineering Manager’s role, they think: “Well, they’re close to the work. Maybe they should just be doing the work? Maybe we don’t need all of them? What value do they actually provide?”   I hear from managers all around me that the number of people reporting to them keeps increasing. Meta is saying a 1-to-50 ratio is their goal, and 15-20 engineers reporting to a manager is becoming very common.   Combine that with the expectation that EMs also ship code, and you quickly start to experience the EM’s role erosion cycle:  Less capacity. You have less capacity to actually manage people.  Less managing. So you do less of the work only you can do. You do fewer 1:1s, postpone career conversations, and don’t deal with team conflicts or processes.   Less value. Which means you provide less value to the engineers reporting to you, and they get used to managing without you.  Less needed. And the less value you provide as a manager, the less ‘needed’ the leader thinks you are. So they increase the engineer-to-manager ratio again.     And this cycle isn’t new. Tech companies get into this delusion that the ‘people stuff’ doesn’t really matter, and then they wake up and quietly start adding back layers:   This trend of getting rid of managers has been tried before.    In 2002, when Google had ~300 engineers, Larry Page and Sergey Brin tried to completely remove all managers. It failed after just a couple of months:  “They relented when too many people went directly to Page with questions about expense reports, interpersonal conflicts, and other nitty-gritty issues. And as the company grew, the founders soon realized that managers contributed in many other, important ways - for instance, by communicating strategy, helping employees prioritize projects, facilitating collaboration, supporting career development, and ensuring that processes and systems aligned with company goals.”  Six years later (with 20k+ employees), Google decided to test again if managers are important. They ran Project Oxygen, which showed that managers did matter (surprise), with good managers strongly correlating with team performance and engineer satisfaction.    And now, Google is flattening again - cutting about 10% of manager, director, and VP roles.   It’s a similar story at Microsoft:   2014 - Satya Nadella announced a ‘major restructuring’: fewer management layers and wider spans of control.   2025 - 11 years later, Microsoft flattened again to ‘increase span of control’.    Layoffs and flattening are most often sudden and make the news headlines, but the recovery is less exciting. No company suddenly hires hundreds of managers, they slowly rebuild those layers over time.    But why? If companies consistently believe that managers are not needed, how come they keep hiring managers again and again?     You can actually run ‘flat’ for a while. It takes a few months or years before companies experience the impact and the pendulum begins to swing back.   What happens is that companies start to accumulate organizational debt - similar to tech debt, a gradual buildup of dysfunction that undermines how good work gets done.   Relational debt is the type of org debt that accumulates the fastest after a flattening. It’s strained, neglected, or transactional relationships where trust and psychological safety erode. When you expand an EM’s role to both be more technical and have more reports, something has to give - you’re chipping away at the people part of the company, and that has consequences.  There’s more negative behavior turning into toxic behavior, more conflicts, and less collaboration.  And that’s even worse with AI:   One of the things managers repeatedly ask me about in workshops is: “How do I keep the team together when they prefer to talk to AI rather than talk to each other?”   So in addition to reduced human contact between managers and employees, engineers are also less in contact with each other.   And once you remove that human connection, you start having more toxic behavior and conflict. And when that conflict occurs, leaders treat it as ‘one bad apple’. The response is often to just get rid of ‘the problematic person’. Well, that person is operating inside an environment, and that poor environment does more damage to your company goals than shipping speed ever makes up for.   Every company has its own problems. When you rip out layers of management, you basically deprioritize people - which will only magnify your existing problems and will make it much harder to deal with the massive change currently happening in the industry.   Senior leaders are getting messages from the market right now. “You can go faster and leaner, you don’t need all those people, use AI and reach your goals faster.”   That makes them anxious, thinking: “Everyone else is doing it, why can’t we?”   The best thing an EM can do is provide grounded reality. The more information we give them, the better decisions they make, and the closer we’ll get to breaking the collective delusion a lot of us are under right now.   Here’s what I suggest to start from:  1. Write it down. Spend time capturing what the real problems are. Get it out of your head so that you can really see them.    It’ll probably not be one or two big problems, but 10-15 smaller ones. Some conflicts between engineers and the PM, engineers not working well together, etc. It’s much easier to come to your manager with a big problem. With 10 small ones, you feel like your already overloaded manager just wouldn’t care.   The next step is to help them care:  2. Attach them to something bigger.    When you’re looking at the 10 little problems, are they all different shapes? Or can you find patterns? If not, how do you convey something that looks small in a way that attaches it to something bigger?   For example, a disagreement between an engineer and the PM. No director wants to hear about that. But the PM ended up not listening to the engineer, so the team built what was asked for and threw most of it away two weeks later. Add to that two engineers who don’t work well together and shipped overlapping implementations of the same thing a week later.   How can you frame that in a way they’ll care about?   Translating the challenges you’re seeing on your teams as obstacles to business goals is always a good move. Think about what your senior leaders care about most. Start with questions like:    What are the company's top priorities?   What does your Director or VP talk about most?   What keeps them up at night?   Then map your list of problems to what your leaders care about. Pick the one that you think is most critical or endangering a current project.    Thanks Suzan for a great conversation and guest article!    To be clear, I'm not saying more management layers are always better, or that there's no benefit in simplifying the chain of command. But there's a big difference between cutting managers because managers don't matter (as many flattening companies claim), and trying to fix your own org structure.   I believe that your first- and second-line engineering managers are often the ones holding the org together. I don’t think it’s a coincidence that just a couple of months after Meta laid off 700 engineering managers, it’s now facing a serious resignation wave.  The Same Side of the Table. As gaming captivates the world, it seems fitting that Grand Theft Auto - its most contradictory, chaotic, and all-encompassing product - is to act as its ambassador. It was hard not to spend the first hour or so of Grand Theft Auto 6's launch day in a kind of stun-lock. As far as video games editorial goes - which is not that far, in fairness; prepare for an over-flattering analogy - the effect was roughly the equivalent of Tom Hanks' experience, as his John H. Miller first set foot on Omaha beach. Tweets and reels whistled overhead, news leads stung the ears, exploding search terms blew apart some poor guides team ally on one side, while new discoveries in the early game - made by the millions and millions of launch-day players all picking it apart at once - appeared by surprise like some flanking ambush on the other. The analogy falls apart pretty quickly when you think about it: the heroism of writing a little article about a video game aside, the frenzy of this week has been a joy, not a horror. But the point is, I've been doing this job for over a decade now, paying attention to video games for another two beyond that, and I've truly never seen anything like this before. It has been totally overwhelming. And then I thought about that for a moment before realising that - duh - nobody has ever seen anything like this before. GTA 6 is the biggest entertainment release of all time, and it's not even remotely close. It's worth taking a moment just to actually, properly take stock of all the headlines from the past couple of days in terms of the sheer breadth and scale of its launch. Parent company Take Two announced yesterday that GTA 6 sold 32.5m copies before it came out. By the end of its first day on sale, it had made a record-obliterating $3.79bn. By contrast, the once record-breaking GTA 5 made a once astounding $800m in the same period; the "opening" period of the largest film of all time, Avengers: Endgame, made $1.22bn, and that's totalling box office receipts across its release day until the end of the first Sunday after it. It has set multiple records for streaming, per StreamCharts, with 214.63m hours watched in its first two days - significantly more than the previous biggest game, Valorant, achieved with 150m hours in its entire launch week. It's garnered more watch time in those two days than Elden Ring, Hogwarts Legacy, and Cyberpunk 2077 achieved with their entire launch weeks combined. Its concurrent viewers peak so far - 6.38 million people - is nearly four times the previous record of 1.74m, again formerly held by Valorant. It crashed Reddit. More than 2 million UK and US Xbox players used the 'New Zealand trick' to play the game early, which is more than a third of that country's entire population. Internet exchange operator DE-CIX claimed its launch led to the highest amount of concurrent internet usage in history, at 33.03 terabits per second. On top of all those raw numbers, it's also just felt utterly inescapable. I can't open Instagram, TikTok, BlueSky or X without being blasted with memes, viral clips of early discoveries, reactions, hot takes, feeble attempts at brand piggybacks, slightly wayward early-game tips from opportunist streamers who haven't escaped the first chapter, or makeup tutorials for looking like Lucia. I can't open my inbox without scrolling through reams of tenuous PR pitches for stories with barely the faintest connection to the game. I can't open my phone without messages from parents, friends or peers. Even the mainstream news - heaven forbid! - has gradually clocked onto this whole video games thing, this unknown artifact from the imaginary world of "online", maybe being a bit important. Dozens of my colleagues have been inundated with last-minute call-ups to provide an expert soundbite (they're so desperate they even got me on at one point). We'll have a lot more to say about this game in the coming days and weeks (with apologies to regulars who are already sick of it - counterprogramming starts this Monday!). It's the richest of texts, a near endless comedy clip generator, a total technical marvel and all the rest - you already know. But it felt worth it to just sit still for a moment, and take stock of what's happening here. This is the single biggest moment any piece of entertainment media has ever had. But more than that it's felt like a kind of party. The vibes in some corners are orgiastic, as streamers uncover spooky twists, outlandish reactivity, and easter eggs I'd never got close to in a hundred-odd hours with the thing - all of this pure dynamite for the audience. Given the budgets involved and the particularly unique blend of circumstances around it - the changing shape of video game funding; of how attention is monopolised; of how development may happen in the future and the sheer amount of time and subsequent anticipation built up since the previous entry - we will likely be waiting decades for another moment like it. If there's ever a moment like it again. Part of the sense of ecstasy going around comes, perhaps subconsciously, from the acknowledgment that in pure hype and attention terms, this might be as good as it ever gets. For the briefest time, the world belongs to video games. Rockstar and Take-Two's executives and shareholders will no doubt reap the greatest rewards from all this - all part of the great irony that makes this game's central premise all the more interesting. But I sincerely hope its developers - especially the 34 fired by the company last year, now awaiting the outcome of their tribunal over alleged union-busting, and those who hope to form a union from the currently open vote - are able to feel a particular sense of pride. Just as this launch has been unprecedented in its success, the last two or three years have been unprecedented in their grimness for video game workers across most of the world, certainly the once-dominat western part. If we're very lucky - and frankly, I have my doubts - this burst of attention and visible profitability might go some way to helping the industry claw its way back, perhaps via attracting, as a knock-on from all the new-found attention, some kind of more sustainable investment. If we're not, and this is really the last behemoth, the last video game monument of its kind, the last rave before the police come raiding at dawn, at least we've gone out with one hell of a bang. GTA 6 - again, it's been said before now - is such a curious thing. A game of goofiness, self-awareness, prestige, pretentiousness, childish humour, astute commentary, ironic cultural criticism, surprising player expression and - above all of that - the most mind-boggling, brain-scrambling level of profoundly human craft. There's something kind of perfect about this. It's a good thing, actually, that video games' greatest export is also its most contradictory. Video games are contradictory things in themselves. If the non-specialist media might still occasionally slip into treating video games like some kind of object from outer space, then we might as well put forward the best possible candidate for a capsule. It's the same way you'd think about it if you had to stick one thing in a vacuum-sealed box, to send out into the universe in an attempt to symbolise humanity: something that summarises close to all of it; that we're proud of; and crucially, that captures the spirit of it too. There are many more that might've put a more respectable foot forward - certainly that have a less chequered history, or maybe a more sophisticated, nuanced, or inventive use of the form. But there's really no better video game for exemplifying the full, chaotic range of the medium. It seems right, when you think about it, for GTA to be the one out there sitting under the spotlight, in the biggest moment this silly, serious artform might ever have. The 29-year-old Gil seemed like a sturdy member of New York’s rotation two years ago. He put together 29 starts of a 3.50 ERA and a 26.8% strikeout rate in 2024. Gil earned AL Rookie of the Year honors for the performance. Gil’s ascension as a mid-rotation starter came to a screeching halt in 2025. Palo Alto Networks said on November 18, 2026, that it agreed to acquire AI infrastructure startup Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, subject to adjustments. The company announced the agreement alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results, and chief executive Nikesh Arora tied the purchase to the way AI is changing security work: “As AI reshapes the threat landscape, we must continually evolve to protect our customers and enable them to adopt AI securely.”  Applied Compute’s platform lets companies take open-weight AI models, whose trained parameters are publicly available, adapt them to their own data and run them in production. That is the opposite of a proprietary model, which a company can only reach through a vendor’s API. Interest in running open models on hardware the buyer controls has spread well past the data center, as one 10-GPU home AI lab shows, and Palo Alto Networks is betting enterprises will want that freedom with security attached. It plans to offer the platform to its own security customers, with deployment in public clouds and in sovereign environments kept inside a country’s borders for data-residency-regulated buyers, while Applied Compute continues serving its existing customers. Arora said on the earnings call that he expects businesses to run a mix of open-weight and proprietary models, and he kept his biggest claim conditional: “If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do.”  He also said Palo Alto Networks first evaluated Applied Compute as a prospective customer, and that its Unit 42 threat intelligence team assessed the platform’s security before the company decided to buy it. The acquisition landed on the same day the company reported fiscal first quarter results for the quarter ended October 31 that beat Wall Street expectations: revenue of $3.44 billion, up 39% from $2.47 billion a year earlier, against $3.31 billion expected on LSEG’s consensus, and adjusted earnings per share of $1.05 versus 97 cents expected. GAAP net income rose to $482 million from $334 million a year earlier. Annual recurring revenue for the next-generation security business climbed 66% to $9.73 billion, and management raised fiscal 2027 guidance to revenue of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion and adjusted EPS of $4.26 to $4.30. Shares rose in extended trading after the two announcements, with readings between just over 7% and 9% depending on when the move was measured, on top of an 85% gain this year heading into the report. It is the company’s second AI acquisition in three months, after September’s purchase of Console, a platform for building agentic workflows. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become co-chief AI officer after the deal closes, and the startup’s research team will join Palo Alto Networks to help train proprietary AI models for use across its products. The transaction is expected to close in the company’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, pending regulatory clearance and customary closing conditions. Jim Goodwin's side are eight games unbeaten, with Zidane Iqbal pivotal Hibernian v Dundee United highlights 21/11/2026 Given the superlatives being thrown in the direction of Zidane Iqbal by the Scottish football fraternity, one would think he was a replica of a certain France great instead of just sharing his name. So much so that BBC Radio Scotland pundits were suggesting on Saturday's Sportsound that the 23-year-old is the answer to Celtic's hunt for a long-term successor to captain Callum McGregor as their midfield general. It is just as well for Dundee United that the Iraq international is tied to them until at least the summer, his early season appearances for Utrecht ruling out a transfer during the January window. So, where has he sprung from and what is all the fuss about? 'Goodwin due a lot of credit and kudos' Hibs 0-4 Dundee United: What Goodwin said Born in Manchester to a Pakistani father and an Iraqi mother, Iqbal came through the Old Trafford youth system. He signed his first professional contract with United in 2021 and became the first British-born South Asian and first-ever British South Asian to play in the Champions League when he came on as an 89th-minute substitute against Young Boys that December. However, that was to be his one and only first-team appearance and, although he had already made his international debut in a World Cup qualifier at the age of 19, he was sold to Utrecht for a reported fee of Â£1m in summer 2023. Starting off in their Jong Utrecht second string, he would go on to make 49 appearances for the Dutch top-flight outfit before making a surprise switch to the Scottish Premiership this summer. On the one hand, United were getting a player who played all three of Iraq's games at this summer's World Cup, two of them starts, albeit all three were heavy defeats. On the other hand, Iqbal had only managed seven appearances last season for Utrecht and had been a second-half substitute in two of their four matches at the start of the new campaign. However, after a pivotal display in what was being described as a midfield "masterclass" by United in Saturday's 4-0 dismantling of hosts Hibernian, manager Jim Goodwin revealed he always had belief the Tangerines were unearthing a "Rolls-Royce". "The head of recruitment's job is to go and identify good talent for us," Goodwin told BBC Scotland. "It's my job to give him the profile and then he goes out and does the groundwork. "We could see immediately when we watched the footage of Zidane and when we had the Zoom call with him and his representatives, we not only had a fantastic player but a really good person with the right characteristics to come and fit the culture here." Zidane Iqbal was also a marked man at the World Cup finals While on-loan Rangers man Lyall Cameron was among the goals and fellow 24-year-old Dylan Tait provided a stylish assist, it was the third leg of what some regard as the best midfield triumvirate in the Premiership who was singled out for most praise at Easter Road. With former Celtic winger Aidan McGeady again pondering the question about McGregor's likely successor, transfer market expert and former United wing-back Allan Preston opined: "A six for Celtic? Look no further than young Iqbal.  "He's been magnificent since he's come to Scottish football, absolutely brilliant. Running the show again. "If Celtic are looking for a young boy at his age with experience, he is a full international, knows the game, played in Scotland, you can see what he can do, there's your man in front of you. "Other players' hair's on fire, but he's just nice and calm. He's at a different level. He doesn't panic. When the ball comes to him, he is so calm on it, he takes his time, he's got great peripheral vision." The former Dundee United wing-back pointed out, though: "He's had his two clubs that he can play for in a year of football, so he is going nowhere until at least the summer, so enjoy him while you can because I think you'll get serious money for this young boy." McGeady pointed to Iqbal's "good pedigree", having started with Manchester United and already having 32 caps for Iraq, but wondered if that would be enough for Celtic to consider him. "I don't even think, if he's performing this well, Celtic will go and get him," said McGeady. "Why are Celtic not looking at players like this? Do they feel they have to prove themselves somewhere else first?" Former Celtic captain Scott Brown was similarly impressed. "He's been a delight to watch - sharpness to get on the ball and willingness to drive forward," the former midfielder and manager pointed out. "He beats a man in the middle of the park as well and there's not too many midfielders willing to do that. "Watching him there talking to the media, he can't get the smile off his face. He enjoys football, he takes the ball under pressure, he does things that other people don't do, especially in midfield. "He brings composure, but he can also drive through as well. His willingness to keep getting on the ball, even if he makes that slight mistake - that's what I really enjoy watching about him." While Goodwin reckons there will be likely interest in the summer, Iqbal has no thoughts of so quickly leaving a club - and manager - who have resurrected his club career. "I'm not even looking at any other clubs," he told BBC Scotland. "I'm fully focused on Dundee United.  "They've given me a platform to enjoy myself and play football. I'm really enjoying my football again. "They've given me faith and confidence. The gaffer and the coaching staff have a lot of belief in me. "The bare minimum I can do is pay them back with strong performances and hopefully it carries on." Iqbal recalled being at Manchester United's "development centre since I was four or five - I signed when I was eight", explaining that he "then left for some first-team football". He stressed that his lack of games last season came as a result of "a couple of injuries" and, while "I learnt a lot in Holland", he is "happy to have left that behind me",  adding: "That book's closed now." Visit our Dundee United page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views Get Dundee United news notifications in the BBC Sport app Iqbal also recalled how Goodwin's enthusiasm persuaded him to make the switch to Tannadice on deadline day.  "After the World Cup, I had one year left on my contract and I was in touch with my agent," the midfielder said. "We both wanted a move and I had a few chats with a few clubs.  "To be fair, I left it a bit late for Dundee United, but after the first call with the gaffer, I straight away called my agent after we ended the call. "I said, 'look, I genuinely feel like the guy really believes in me'. "It happened very late. I had to drive from Holland to Scotland. It was a tough drive but worth it in the end." That World Cup was also a defining experience, with representing his country in the United States described as surreal. "Having your friends and family there to watch you and playing on the world stage, with so many people, was a dream," he said. "Playing against top players gave me that confidence boost I needed. I thought I did well in the three tough games. "I knew, wherever I'd end up, with the faith of the gaffer, I could really kick on and push because I've learnt so much from the World Cup." Goodwin is the manager to have done that and Iqbal added: "He's such a top guy, not just in football.  "His tactics are amazing. Everyone's comfortable. Everyone wants to fight for him."
