Donate today  Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations A fight over rent control rules erupted in Jersey City this month, after progressive city council members pushed legislation to protect tenants of a downtown development from a rent hike — a move that ended with the bill getting tossed before it could be formally introduced. The battle started when the owner of a waterfront high-rise paid off the building’s mortgage early, causing existing affordable housing protections for hundreds of units to expire. The protections came in exchange for state financing of the building decades ago. Tenants were warned that rents would spike to market rate, sparking outcry and spurring the councilmembers to introduce an ordinance they said would protect people on the verge of being priced out of their homes. But the measure proposed by Councilmember Jake Ephros, a democratic socialist who took office in January, was financially unsound, according to critics and other officials. With only Ephros and fellow democratic socialist Joel Brooks supporting, the nine-member council declined to entertain the bill. Now pro-development groups are claiming a win against rent control in a city that is rapidly gentrifying. It’s been 40 years since ground broke on Newport, a master-planned community developed by the LeFrak Organization and the Simon Property Group. The neighborhood sprawls over hundreds of acres on Jersey City’s waterfront, right above the Holland Tunnel. It’s land that was a derelict railyard bolstered by landfill. Today there’s a mall, a row of high-rise hotels and office buildings, restaurants, parks and even a heliport. The Presidential Plaza towers were the first residential buildings at Newport, and they were financed through a New Jersey Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency program that required a portion of the units be affordable to low-income and moderate-income tenants. That protection was in place for the life of the loan so when LeFrak decided to pay off the debt early, it was no longer bound by the income restrictions. “ This year, we were in a position where we could prepay the mortgage. We wanted to refinance it so that we could pay for and finance building renovations,” said Charles Burton, LeFrak’s head of government and community relations. After paying off the mortgage, LeFrak informed tenants in September that below-market rents would only be available for one more lease. Rents would rise to market rate in subsequent leases. The move was something LeFrak had warned city officials in recent years was coming. The developer had offered to extend the affordable housing protections on the towers last year as part of a new tax abatement deal, but the city council overwhelmingly rejected the proposal. Newport tenants said they feared being priced out of their homes and they called on city leaders to help them. Ephros, a political newcomer who ran for council last year as a democratic socialist, responded to the Newport situation with an ordinance that would change Jersey City’s rent control law to eliminate a lifetime exemption for developments built in a designated redevelopment area. “This is about more than Newport,” he said. “This is about tackling skyrocketing housing costs and moving just a step closer to winning housing as a human right.” There are dozens of redevelopment areas across Jersey City, all designated by the Jersey City Redevelopment Agency, that are places where builders are incentivized to invest in struggling neighborhoods. Newport is built in one of those areas, but has long since ceased to be an area in need of investment. About 100 municipalities across New Jersey have some form of rent control. The state law that allows for rent control exempts new construction for 30 years. Jersey City’s local rules give new construction in redevelopment areas a lifetime exemption. “ The deal was that if developers come in and build housing, they would in return get the ability to have rent control exemption indefinitely,” said Ben LoPiccolo, the CEO of the development firm BLDG-UP and the president of the Jersey City Apartment Owners Association. “That was what gave them the incentive to take the risk to invest the money in a city like Jersey City.” Nicholas Kikis, the vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs for the New Jersey Apartment Association, said the lifetime exemption was critical for allowing developers to recover the costs of high-rise construction. “ When you're talking about redevelopment projects, they are significant projects, often significantly vertical,” Kikis said. “We're talking about luxury towers, and this is not the type of project that recovers its entire cost basis in a thirty-year time period.” Mayor James Solomon said he was skeptical that the ordinance was financially sound. He worried about potentially discouraging development at a time when Jersey City faces a deep fiscal crisis. “ We're not at a place right now as a city where we can afford tens of millions of dollars of loss to our tax base, particularly from some of the biggest developers in the city,” Solomon said. But Ephros noted that other cities and towns which don’t offer the lifetime exemption have been able to sustain their own redevelopment efforts. “ We have had decades and decades, 40-plus years of rent control in New Jersey, and we have not seen evidence of a collapse in property taxes or a collapse in property values that leads to this massive shift in the burden of property taxes,” Ephros said. “We just haven't seen that.” Ephros’s ordinance was not the first time the redevelopment area exemption was targeted. A similar measure was introduced by the city council in 2019, but never received a final vote. The new measure, at least in its current form, won't ever get a vote. Councilmember Eleana Little, who represents Newport and often aligns with Ephros and Brooks, abstained despite previously voicing support. The council members who voted against advancing the measure said they sympathized with the Newport tenants, but didn't have enough information about the potential effects of ending the exemption. Thomas Zuppa, the member representing Journal Square, called the measure a potential “monumental shift” in city policy. “ I live in a redevelopment zone in Journal Square with a landlord who raised my rent,” Zuppa said. “I have to set aside my own personal interest for the betterment of the city. Journal Square's had some lean years there for about four decades, and we're finally seeing some growth and development infrastructure built. So I wouldn't want to put us in a position where we're hampering that at this point without the appropriate studies.” Councilmember Jake Ephros proposed a bill that critics said was financially unsound. Though the proposal that would place the Newport towers under rent control is stalled, new affordable housing protections for tenants at the properties could be on the way. Solomon announced Thursday that city hall had reached a deal with LeFrak for a new payment-in-lieu-of-taxes (PILOT) agreement. As part of the deal, LeFrak would increase the number of affordable units in the Newport towers from 272 to 299, with some offering rents at $1,000 a month. The proposed tax abatements would last for 30 years. Under the proposed financial agreement, the affordable housing protections would remain in place for the full 30-year term, even if LeFrak voluntarily ended its tax exemption early. “ We want to protect our residents. We want to keep them in our homes,” Burton said. “They're very much a great part of our community, but affordable housing is a public-private partnership, and we just hope that the city government works with us to accomplish this goal for everyone.” Burton said LeFrak and the Solomon administration began negotiating the deal in October, the same time that Newport tenants were pressuring city leaders for help. “Families at Newport were told this fall that their rents were going to market rate,” Solomon said. “Many of them had no idea where they would go. Because of these agreements, they get to stay, and get to stay at affordable monthly rents.” The new proposal must be approved by the city council. The pair of ordinances being considered are on the agenda to be introduced at next week’s meeting. “ It gives me no joy to offer LeFrak a tax abatement,” Ephros said. “But my duty is to protect these tenants who are fighting for their homes. And if this is the only way because we are not able to, this time, bring the building under rent control, I'm willing to entertain it if the deal is right.” LeFrak had been on the verge of a similar deal with the city last year, after negotiations with former Mayor Steve Fulop. But the city council rejected it by a large majority. Ephros and Brooks said they intend to bring back the proposal to end the redevelopment area exemption as expanding rent control remains a core part of the democratic socialist platform. It’s unclear when, or how it might be amended to win over skeptical council members. Developers pledged to fight any future version of the ordinance. “ I don't think there's anything you can change about the proposal to make me feel comfortable,” LoPiccolo said. “I think that when you really dig deep into any proposal that eliminates the rent control exemptions and you truly do an impact study on what will happen if that happens, it will really create a disaster for real estate here in Jersey City.” Ephros cast the ordinance’s defeat as a learning lesson. He noted the recent win for rent control advocates in Elizabeth came after years of organizing and campaigning in that city. “ I see this as a first step,” Ephros said. “We understand a lot more of the terrain that we're going to have to deal with.” Correction: A previous version of this story misstated how long affordable housing protections would remain in place under the proposed tax abatements. The protections would last for the full 30-year term. There is enough justified anger among the British youth to spark a wave of mass protests. Save Share The protests engulfing Europe represent a new level of popular mobilisation quite unlike any historical precedent. In France, Spain, Italy, Serbia, Germany and other countries across the continent, mass movements are challenging austerity and government failures. On Friday, the United Kingdom saw what is likely to be the beginning of its own wave of youth-driven demonstrations. Thousands of students walked out of hundreds of schools and universities around the country, from Aberdeen to Brighton, Swansea to Nottingham, making it one of the largest student mobilisations since the tripling of tuition fees back in 2010.     The protests were called by organisations involved in the International Conference Against War, a pan-European initiative aimed at coordinating the movements against militarism. The University and College Union (UCU) was the first union to back the initiative with a National Day of Action, urging members across the university sector to hold protests and rallies alongside students. That major unions followed UCU in supporting the walkouts, including Unison, Unite, the National Education Union (NEU), GMB and the Educational Institute of Scotland (EIS), speaks to the potential of union support. In London, demonstrations from universities and colleges converged on Trafalgar Square to chants of “fight for our future, not their wars” before moving to Downing Street to hear student activists and trade union leaders berate the government for prioritising defence spending over education and public services. There is indeed much for British youth to be angry about. Like in the rest of Europe, young people in the UK are facing a convergence of high inflation, unemployment, economic stagnation, the gutting of public services and deteriorating living standards, including a housing crisis stoked by property speculation. Combined with police brutality over solidarity with Palestine, unrestrained racism and sexism and expectations of environmental and climate catastrophe, mass protest is rather predictable. According to government estimates, close to one million people between 16 and 24 years of age are “Neets” – not in education, employment or training; this is more than 13 percent of that age group. Young people make up more than 40 percent of the unemployed in the country. Apart from a tough job market, there is also a rampant mental health epidemic and an education system that few can afford. Here we have the makings of a social and economic crisis waiting to happen, and yet the government response has been to seek more austerity. It is a wonder that Alan Milburn, former Labour minister responsible for introducing private finance into the NHS in the late 1990s, was commissioned to write the controversial report on Neets for the government. Why bother to provide welfare when the private sector can solve the crisis? Unsurprisingly, Milburn’s recommendations are market-focused and include cutting certain benefits for youth, including for those with disabilities. This comes on top of years of austerity in the higher education sector. Job cuts and course closures have become standard responses from university managements dealing with the lack of direct government funding. Many describe it as academic vandalism. What funding cuts have produced is extreme dysfunction, chaos and mismanagement: Faustian bargains with banks, management consultants and corporate outsourcing that serve efficiency and profit over quality provision. While education and civilian job openings are dwindling, British youth are offered more opportunities in the army, which is now promoting a fully paid 18-month “foundation scheme”. Military training, bolstered by a public campaign around “warfighting readiness” as part of last year’s Strategic Defence Review, was the brainchild of ministers under Keir Starmer, one of the most unpopular prime ministers in British history. True to form, Starmer pushed through an additional 15 billion pounds ($19.6bn) towards defence immediately before leaving office, for a total of 298 billion pounds ($389.8bn) over four years. This is a worrying trend across Europe: While there are diminishing funds for public services, military spending is shooting up. This fact has not been lost on young people. But what is driving this rearmament frenzy is that the European project is increasingly being bound together by NATO, along with Trump’s insistence that the EU should pay its fair share in maintaining the alliance. Support for Ukraine against Russia is at the centre of that project. If youth mobilisation in the UK reaches the same level as in France, for example, this could be the first major test of Andy Burnham’s government. The French revolt was started over education – not the first strikes in French history over education, considering the origins of the 1968 uprisings. Still, France spends 5.1 percent of GDP on education. The UK spends 4.1 percent of GDP on education, and even part of this budget has been diverted to defence, with less funding for schools in the coming years. The UK has had seven prime ministers in the past decade, each one unable to deliver desperately needed income and wealth redistribution. A decade of Tory prime ministers allowed the rich to get very rich. Starmer continued the tradition. He was hammered by Reform and the Greens in the last local elections, firstly because he was unable to come through on the social democratic promises that many were hoping a Labour government would provide. But second, he failed to recognise the genuine anger over British complicity in the Palestinian genocide, and then responded to mass protest with punitive legislation. Notwithstanding the Burnham bounce, the sitting prime minister has stuck to the same tack as his predecessor. His new foreign secretary has admitted that the government got it wrong over Palestine, but this needs to be backed up by action. As Burnham faces growing protest, a heavy-handed approach will not work. Nor will more neoliberal reforms. A half-century of privatisation, deregulation and cuts to social welfare has produced the current malaise, and the crisis is only deepening. The youth and the rest of European society are demanding change – real, lasting change in the political and economic spheres. The revolutions that convulsed Europe in 1848 were a response to severe economic crisis, unemployment and bad harvests that caused famine. The European protests today unfold under comparable conditions. The task of those who want to see change is an internationalism that can generalise grievances, coordinate the movements and deliver concrete solidarity against austerity and war. Harvard CS 2881R  Fall 2026 |             Fall 2025 archive  Everyone who wants to be considered for the course must fill out the Fall 2026 course registration form. In-person attendance will be mandatory for students enrolled in the course. Read Homework Zero HW0 is due August 5, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. Submitting Homework Zero is a necessary but not sufficient condition for admission to the course. Completing the assignment does not guarantee admission. To get a sense of the issues we will cover, please read It’s 2030 and we fucked up. How did it happen? and All Watched Over. Fall 2026, Thursdays 3:45pm–6:30pm Eastern Time (first lecture September 3) Classroom: Room 2112, 114 Western Avenue, Allston, MA 02134 (building information and directions) Instructor: Boaz Barak Teaching Fellows: Natalia Siwek, Terry Zhou, Michael Shoemate, Ege Çakar, Itay Lavie, Lia Zheng, and Hugh Van Deventer Course email: cs2881@boazbarak.org Course Description: This is a graduate-level course on challenges in the alignment and safety of artificial intelligence. We will consider technical questions as well as societal and other impacts of the field. Prerequisites: We require mathematical maturity and proficiency with proofs, probability, and information theory, along with the foundations of machine learning at the level of an undergraduate course such as Harvard CS 181 or MIT 6.036. On the applied side, students should be comfortable programming in Python and training a basic neural network. The course will have 13 in-person lectures. Each lecture will also involve discussion and the presentation of an experiment by a group of students. Attendance: In-person attendance is mandatory. Students are expected to attend all lectures, do the reading in advance, and discuss the readings in an electronic forum. AI use: Students are allowed and encouraged to use generative and agentic AI as much as they can for studying, exploring concepts, and completing their assignments and projects. We will explore ways to either give students access to compute credits or reimburse compute expenses. Electronic device policy: Students can use laptops in class, but we will ask those using them to sit in the back so they do not distract other students. Assignments: The course will involve the following assignments: presenting an experiment in class, writing scribe notes, completing a final project, and potentially completing one or more homework assignments or mini-projects. Grading will be decided later. Lecture recordings: To the extent technically possible, we intend to record and publish the lectures online, though there might be some delay in doing so. Note that recording is done automatically by a static in-room camera, and some parts of the lecture (e.g., whiteboard work or discussions) may not be captured as well. In addition, we will honor requests by external speakers not to record their talks. POTENTIAL CONFLICT OF INTEREST NOTE: In addition to his position at Harvard, Boaz is also a member of the technical staff at OpenAI. The course will include discussions of models from multiple providers, including OpenAI, and students are also encouraged to use AIs from multiple providers while doing their work. If students in the course have any concerns about this conflict, please do not hesitate to contact Boaz, the other staff, or the Harvard SEAS administration. For what it is worth, I (Boaz) will see it as a great success of the course if its graduates work in AI safety in any capacity, including in academia, nonprofits, governments, or any of OpenAI’s competitors. Additional lecture topics and materials will be added as they are confirmed. Kraken said all orders were processed correctly and found no evidence of a security breach or compromised accounts. Crypto exchange Kraken said it would honor trades executed during a sharp selloff across its Canadian-dollar markets that briefly pushed Bitcoin to the equivalent of about $17,000 on Saturday. In a statement, Kraken said its Canadian-dollar trading pairs experienced heavy selling pressure starting around 20:00 UTC on Friday, causing prices to fall significantly below those on other markets. The exchange said every order was processed correctly and its security teams found no evidence of a breach or compromised accounts. “Executed trades stand,” Kraken said. Kraken’s BTC/CAD pair fell to $24,250 Canadian during the 15-minute interval beginning at 08:00 UTC on Saturday, according to exchange trading data. On Friday, the Bank of Canada’s reference rate showed C$1.4325 per US dollar, putting Bitcoin’s low on Kraken’s Canadian-dollar market at about $16,900. This was about 71% below Bitcoin’s price of around $57,650 on Kraken’s BTC/USD market during the same five-minute interval. Blockstream CEO Adam Back suggested that a market maker on Kraken’s USD/CAD spot market may have exhausted its funds, causing prices to diverge from broader foreign exchange rates. Back said arbitrage subsequently spread the pricing distortion to other Canadian-dollar trading pairs. Kraken has not confirmed Back’s proposed explanation. Cointelegraph reached out to Kraken for comments but did not receive a response before publication. Onchain FX does not need to recreate the trillion-dollar institutional market to become useful. Real demand can make smaller markets work first. Opinion by Michael Egorov, founder of Curve Finance and Yield Basis For a long time, the obvious way to think about onchain foreign exchange (FX) was to start at the top. Banks tokenize currencies, large financial institutions move their FX activity onchain and institutional liquidity naturally follows. The end result? Blockchain-based FX eventually grows large enough to resemble its traditional counterpart. But that’s not necessarily how it is going to happen. In fact, there are growing signs that onchain FX will develop in the exact opposite way — from the bottom up. Stablecoins like Brazilian Digital (BRZ) or Monerium’s EURe can be quickly redeemed onchain and easily moved from digital wallets to bank accounts. They generate healthy trading activity as decentralized finance (DeFi) users swap them in decentralized exchange (DEX) pools. Markets like this end up developing in real time around a practical user need, which is moving directly between digital currencies and fiat. This is still just an early-stage example, but the use case and demand are real enough. Keyrock data shows that the majority of onchain stablecoin trades tied to emerging market currencies fall in the $1,000 to $10,000 range — modest amounts compared to institutional scale — but that’s precisely the point. It shows how the market is building in the general direction of onchain FX to meet practical payment needs, not just large traders. People and businesses need to move their money between currencies, and clearly, they are not content to wait for major traditional finance (TradFi) institutions to move their FX operations onto blockchain rails. Related: Paraguay bank collapse shows stablecoins can offer a lifeline... of sorts There’s a pretty common assumption about onchain FX in that a market needs huge liquidity before it can become really useful. In practice, though, that’s not entirely true. If there is genuine demand from someone who needs to exchange dollars into euros, Swiss francs or another currency, even a smaller pool can process those transactions and serve a real economic purpose. Stablecoin DEX Trade Volume. Source: Keyrock Research Onchain FX doesn’t need to become big before it becomes useful; instead, it can grow precisely because people are actually using it. As a matter of fact, this is more or less what happened with stablecoins. They began as a relatively niche crypto-native use case, and yet today we already know them to be part of a much broader financial infrastructure. Chainalysis recently shared data that shows cross-border stablecoin activity jumped to over $220 billion by mid-2026. That’s an almost 80% growth over the course of one year, proving that demand and activity are constantly on the rise. There is no reason onchain FX can’t follow a similar path. This is actually the most practical side of this issue. Onchain FX obviously won’t be able to compete with the entire global foreign exchange market anytime soon; that’s still years away. But the more interesting question is what problems it can solve for someone who already has money onchain. Today, you can exchange a USD stablecoin into a EUR stablecoin (or some other alternative) onchain and use that money for payments with relatively little trouble. In fact, doing it this way is often faster and cheaper than going with a classic international bank transfer. Related: Circle’s ARC token sale lifts earnings as lower yields weigh on USDC income The same logic applies to onchain FX. A fintech or crypto-card company does not need to recreate the entire institutional market; what they need is to move their customers’ funds efficiently between currencies. When someone is trying to pay in a different currency, converting it can add costs to the operation, since it usually involves Visa or Mastercard, which charge around 1% in processing fees. Onchain exchanges are a much better option here. If user funds are already living on blockchain rails, swapping USD stablecoins into EUR stablecoins can be done directly, without going through any extra intermediaries, which is both faster and less costly. Banks will most likely remain important entry and exit points where digital money needs to interact with the real world. Issuing and redeeming local currencies, accessing bank accounts, dealing with compliance and such is where banks will take the lead. But when the money is actually onchain, many of the traditional “in-between” steps can be dropped for greater efficiency. From the perspective of a user who just wants to conduct a financial transfer with minimal complications, that’s a highly positive improvement. How big or small the overall market matters little in this case. There is, of course, a catch. Real demand is crucial, but it does not magically solve the problem of liquidity. The challenge is not simply to create a EUR/USD or CHF/USD pool; it’s to make them economically sustainable. This is where automated market makers can make a difference. Traditional market-making firms may not find it attractive to provide liquidity for a small FX market; there may simply not be enough volume to justify the operational costs. Cross-border stablecoin flows. Source: Chainalysys Automated liquidity changes that equation because software can provide liquidity continuously without requiring a market-making firm to manually manage every trade. Imagine two dollar stablecoins, USDC (USDC) and Tether (USDT). From the perspective of a traditional exchange, moving from one dollar stablecoin into another might look like a fairly boring business. Both assets are supposed to be worth roughly $1, so there isn’t much price movement to trade around. But if there is still a real need for people to switch between stablecoins like that, an automated market maker can create a pool where users can make that swap directly. Each trade generates a small fee for the liquidity providers, and when enough people need the same conversion, a market can exist even when it doesn’t look particularly exciting to a traditional market maker. This kind of adoption cannot exactly be called explosive, true, but there’s also nothing wrong with slow, natural growth. Sometimes, new markets just need a small group of people who have a problem the existing infrastructure does not solve particularly well. If those users can make the market economically viable, liquidity can grow from there. About the author: Michael Egorov is the founder of Curve Finance and Yield Basis. He is also a physicist, entrepreneur and crypto maximalist. Michael transitioned from the scientific field to the crypto industry and holds a bronze medal from the International Physics Olympiad and a PhD in ultracold atoms. This 1953 Hudson Hornet Club Coupe was previously part of the Art Astor collection, and it reportedly underwent a refurbishment completed in 2008. Power is provided by a 308ci inline-six with a 308 head and a Twin H-Power induction system, and the car is finished in turquoise and white over a color-coordinated interior. Additional elements include chrome wire-spoke wheels and whitewall tires as well as an independent front suspension, a four-speed Hydra-Matic automatic transmission, hood and fender ornaments, a push-button radio, and a Weather Control heater with a cowl vent. This Hornet was acquired by the current owner in 2024 and is now offered by the seller on their behalf in Nevada with a clean Montana title in the name of the owner’s LLC.  The car is said to have been brought to bare metal during a refurbishment completed in 2008 under previous ownership, and it was repainted turquoise with a white roof. The “step-down” chassis uses a floor pan that is attached to the bottom of the frame rails, thus increasing interior headroom. Exterior features include a split windshield, a driver-side mirror, full-length rub rails, bright window trim and rocker-panel moldings, and chrome bumpers with guards.  The 15″ Tru-Spoke chrome wire wheels were installed in 2016 and are wrapped in whitewall tires. Coil-spring independent suspension is fitted up front along with semi-elliptical leaf springs out back. Braking comes from drums at all four corners.  The seats were retrimmed in turquoise and white leather during the aforementioned refurbishment, and they are accompanied by matching door panels and black carpeting. A swing-out tray is located under the dash, and amenities include a Weather Control heater, a push-button radio, a locking glovebox,  sun visors, a fold-down rear armrest, dome lights, and bright doorsill trim.  A three-spoke steering wheel with a semi-circular chrome horn ring fronts a round 115-mph speedometer and a matching clock set to either side of a horizontal bar with gauges for coolant temperature and fuel level, the latter of which is inoperative. The five-digit odometer shows 690 miles, and total mileage is unknown.  The Twin H-Power induction system was created for the purpose of homologating Hudson’s 308ci inline-six for NASCAR and AAA stock-car racing, where it proved dominant from 1951 through 1954. Introduced to the consumer market as an optional package in 1952, it employed dual downdraft Carter one-barrel carburetors to produce 160 horsepower and 260 lb-ft of torque. A tubular header is fitted and linked to a replacement exhaust system, and the seller states that the engine is believed to have been rebuilt under previous ownership.  Power is routed to the rear wheels through a four-speed Hydra-Matic automatic transmission. The seller states that the transmission and rear differential were rebuilt during prior ownership. The DJI Mini 5 Pro puts a 1-inch, 50 MP camera into a 249.9-gram drone, and the Mini 4 Pro it replaces still shoots through a sensor two classes smaller. The upgrade is real. Price is where it gets strange, since DJIâs own US store doesnât sell the Mini 5 Pro at all this season. American buyers order it through authorized resellers, while the Mini 4 Pro fades off DJIâs shelf and lingers at retail with discounts. So the comparison runs on two tracks. Launched on September 17, 2025, the Mini 5 Pro took the slot the Mini 4 Pro held for two years as the default small drone for serious travel footage. This holiday, the choice between them is a camera decision and a shopping decision at once. A 1-inch CMOS sensor with 50 MP and an f/1.8 lens at 24 mm equivalent sits in the Mini 5 Pro, the largest sensor DJI has fitted to a drone in this weight class. The Mini 4 Pro answers with less. Its 1/1.3-inch CMOS shoots 48 MP through an f/1.7 lens, and it built its reputation on 4K/60 HDR video and 4K/100 slow motion from that smaller sensor. Sensor size decides the low-light footage, since the bigger sensor gathers more light per pixel and holds detail when the smaller one starts to smear. Daylight narrows the gap, and both drones shoot travel footage that clients accept. Amazon: DJI Mini 5 Pro Fly More Combo with DJI RC 2Price: $1,099Where to buy: Buy on Amazon Flight time runs 36 minutes on the Mini 5 Proâs standard battery and 52 minutes on the Plus battery, and it stores 42 GB internally before a card goes in. The Mini 4 Pro flies 34 minutes standard and 45 minutes on its Plus battery, close enough that battery count decides a shooting day. Flight time is a tie. Sensing splits them harder, since the Mini 5 Pro adds LiDAR nightscape obstacle sensing for low-light flying at this weight. Both send video over DJIâs O4 family link at up to 20 km, the newer drone on O4+ and the older one on O4. Internal storage counts on real shoots, since 42 GB covers a morning of clips before a card swap. The Mini 4 Pro leans on cards sooner. That storage gap shows up on travel days far more than a spec sheet comparison suggests at first glance. The Mini 5 Pro can shoot a full morning on internal memory and still land with room to spare. A Mini 4 Pro ownerâs day runs through a card wallet instead, plus a running mental count of what each card still holds. Cards cost little, but a forgotten card ends a shoot before it starts, and it happens to careful people. Both drones live under the 250-gram line in standard form, the Mini 5 Pro at 249.9 grams give or take 4 grams and the Mini 4 Pro under 249 grams. That line is the whole category. Staying under it keeps both drones in the lightest regulatory class and in any camera bag, which is why this comparison exists at all. Plus batteries bend the rule, since the longer packs push weight up as flight time climbs toward those 52 and 45 minute figures. Pick the standard packs if the weight class counts for you. DJIâs US store doesnât list the Mini 5 Pro, so American buyers go through authorized resellers, where kits start at $759 and climb through $959 and $1,099 to $1,159. The Mini 4 Pro launched at $759 with the RC-N2 controller, $959 with the RC 2 and $1,099 in Fly More form, and DJIâs store now shows it out of stock. Retailers still carry the older drone, some at a discount. Kits run four deep on the newer drone, and the Fly More Combo at $1,099 bundles the RC 2 controller with three batteries for long shooting days. A discounted Mini 4 Pro is the value play this winter. That split changes the advice, since the newer droneâs price is firm everywhere while the older oneâs price moves with each retailerâs remaining stock. Shop the older drone like a clearance item and the newer one like a launch item. Owners of the Mini 4 Pro face the harder call of the two, since their drone still handles almost everything casual flying asks of it on a normal day. The upgrade buys low-light headroom, stronger sensing and built-in storage, not a new category of shot. First-time buyers skip that debate entirely and start from the newer sensor. Amazon: DJI Mini 4 Pro with DJI RC 2Price: $959Where to buy: Buy on Amazon The tradeoff is sensor against savings: the Mini 5 Pro shoots cleaner footage in worse light, and the Mini 4 Pro leaves hundreds of dollars in your pocket for batteries, filters and travel. Weight stays legal and light on both, at 249.9 grams for the newer drone and under 249 grams for the older one in standard form. Choose once, fly for years. The Mini 5 Pro is the dawn, dusk and indoor pick: the 1-inch sensor and the LiDAR sensing justify their premium every time the light drops. The Mini 4 Pro at a discount still delivers in daylight, and the savings buy spare batteries. A current Mini that still flies straight needs no replacement; this generation gap shows in footage, not in flight feel. You can tell a lot about someone from the things on their desk that didn’t come with the job. A photo leaning against the monitor, the pen they won’t lend out, a lamp they switch on when the overhead lights get to be too much. None of those things need to match. In fact, a desk often starts to feel more like yours when you stop trying to make everything match. The eight picks here make room for different parts of your day. A retro speaker gives pixel art a screen of its own, while a photo printer doubles as a frame for a picture you’d rather not leave buried on your phone. There’s a LEGO orchid for anyone who likes building things by hand, and a modular monitor stand concept that makes a case for arranging your desk around what you actually reach for.   The Altar I gets away with a red volume knob because almost everything around it is black. Designed by Andrew Emerson for Electronic Materials Office, the mechanical keyboard puts expressive lettering and sculpted keycaps inside an aluminum body just 15 mm tall. Some groups of keys are raised, others are flat or recessed, so there’s a physical distinction between them as well as a visual one. It’s the kind of keyboard you pick because you care what the numbers look like. There’s a practical reason to like it, too. A physical switch moves between two remembered Bluetooth devices, handy if your work laptop and personal computer share the same desk. The stock Kailh Choc V1 Red switches are linear, meaning there’s no deliberate tactile bump in the keystroke, and you can swap them for others in the Choc V1 family.   Most pens spend their time out of sight or disappearing under a notebook. Novium’s Levitating Pen 3.0, also called the Hoverpen Future, gives you a reason to put it back. The pen balances on a point at a 60-degree angle inside a magnetic pedestal, with no battery or cable involved. Give the barrel a twist, and it spins in place. It’s a small object, but that diagonal does a surprising amount of work against the right angles of a monitor and keyboard. It is available in rollerball and fountain pen versions, plus a configuration that lets you change between the two by swapping the grip section. That choice matters more than the magnetic trick if you already have a preference about how you write. The rollerball takes a Schmidt 888 refill, while the fountain version can use bottled ink with a converter. It makes the most sense beside a notebook you reach for often. If you rarely write by hand, you’re mostly buying the pedestal and the show. Click Here to Buy Now: $149.00 Black Friday: Free $20 calendar with every order   Divoom’s Astrotoo looks like a computer from the era when a joystick belonged next to the screen. The rounded case sits on a roughly 4.2 by 4.3-inch footprint, with three raised keys, a joystick, and an orange back button that do more than sell the retro look. They handle music and display functions without sending you back to your phone for every adjustment. Divoom positions the 20-watt speaker for close listening, which makes more sense here than trying to fill a room from the corner of a desk. The 3.95-inch square display makes the Astrotoo worth a look even if you already have a speaker. You can put a pixel animation on it, choose a clock face, or give a favorite photo the little screen to itself. The last option might be the most personal, particularly if the big screen beside it is full of windows you’d rather close. You’ll need Divoom’s app to customize the display, though the physical controls take over for everyday use.   Masafumi Ishikawa’s Rolling World Clock turns a time zone check into something you do with your hand. Rotate its 12-sided body until the city you want is at the top, and the single hour hand shows the time for that city’s standard offset. The case is barely over three inches across, so it can sit beside a monitor without looking like a second display. And unlike a world clock app, it leaves the city you picked right there in front of you. This is the clock to choose if the other time zone means something to you. Leave it on Tokyo because that’s where your sister lives, or turn it to Los Angeles before calling a friend. Ishikawa’s design is better at answering “Are they likely to be awake?” than telling you exactly when a meeting starts. It has no minute hand, covers only the 12 marked time zones, and doesn’t account for daylight saving time. Keep your phone handy when the exact time matters. Click Here to Buy Now: $60.00 Black Friday: Free $20 calendar with every order   Lorenzo Vega’s Modular Monitor Stand starts with a familiar problem: a phone stand, a pen tray and a document holder can each tidy one thing while making the desk feel more crowded together. Vega’s working concept moves those jobs onto a rack that clamps to the back edge of the desk. Five interchangeable tray designs fit onto two horizontal rails, with options for stationery, a phone or tablet, and upright papers. Raising the monitor leaves the surface below open for a notebook or reference book. The layout is the part worth borrowing, even if you never get your hands on the stand itself. Someone who works from printed notes could put the document holder right beside the screen. Someone who sketches could give that spot to a tray for pencils and keep the space below clear for an open pad. Vega’s design puts the things you reach for on the same structure, but it doesn’t decide which of those things matters most. That’s a useful distinction for any desk organizer.   The top of the Anywhere-Use Lamp is also its switch. Press anywhere around the rim to turn it on or cycle through four brightness settings. TENT and Fujita Metal’s design, sold in Japan as the Table Lamp ICHI, hides four AA batteries inside a narrow stem, with the cap and base unscrewing for transport. There’s no cable dictating which corner it goes in. With a base about four inches across, it can go where the light makes sense, even if that isn’t near an outlet. The warm light suits a desk that doubles as a place to read or draw once the laptop is shut. Use a lower setting for a little light beside the monitor, then move the lamp closer to the page when you want it there instead. There’s a substantial payoff for turning down the brightness: with rechargeable Eneloop AAs, the maker estimates about 80 hours on the lowest setting but only eight on the highest. It’s a lamp you can move freely, though you’ll want spare batteries if you keep it bright. Click Here to Buy Now: $149.00 Black Friday: Free $20 calendar with every order   Polaroid’s Hi-Print 3×3 earns its spot by doing something most printers don’t: giving you somewhere to put the picture. It turns photos from your phone into three-inch squares, and the printer itself doubles as a frame. Slide a print into the front, and the plain white housing recedes behind whatever you chose to put there. A trip photo or a blurry snapshot of the dog can stay in view all day without becoming another thing you have to wake up or swipe past. Polaroid’s iOS and Android app lets you add templates, stickers, and borders before printing. You can also leave the image alone and let the square crop do the editing. The printer makes more sense if you like to rotate what’s on display or print extras for other people. For one picture you already love and intend to keep there, a simple frame is the better buy. The Hi-Print’s value is in making it easy to change your mind about what goes in it.   LEGO’s Mini Orchid is a 274-piece build with five peach blooms, a few closed buds, and a terracotta-colored pot on a wood-effect stand. The buds make the arrangement look less uniform, while the pot and its little platform give it the proportions of something you’d see on a windowsill. It has enough color to break up a run of gray electronics without asking you to redesign the desk around it. And a desk nowhere near a window will suit it fine. The time spent building it is part of what makes it feel personal. You could buy a convincing artificial orchid and be done in seconds, but here you put together the pot, leaves, and flowers before deciding where they’ll live. Check the vertical space before you commit to a spot: the finished model stands over 10 inches tall, so “mini” doesn’t mean it’ll tuck under a low shelf. It may look better out at the edge of the desk anyway, where the flowers have room around them. On a crowded desk, the best first change might be to swap something out rather than find room for one more object. Replace the keyboard you already use every day, or move a lamp to the side where you actually open your notebook. If the practical side of your setup is already sorted, give the one remaining spot to something with no obligation to help you get through your inbox. A desk can look pulled together without looking like it came as a set. The clock can stay turned toward someone else’s city. The photo can change next week. The little orchid can keep its spot even when the notebook and monitor move. Those details make the space feel inhabited. A Wealth of Common Sense Posted November 22, 2026 by Ben Carlson Four letter words have many different connotations. Sometimes you say them when you’re mad. Sometimes when you’re happy. Sometimes when you’re surprised or sad or confused or scared or some other emotion. Risk is a four letter word in finance. Sometimes it’s a good thing — risk premium. Sometimes it’s a strategy — risk management. Sometimes it’s a number — risk-adjusted returns. Sometimes it’s a warning label — risk of loss. Right now the risk of loss is a reality. S&P 500 is now in correction territory: The chart looks like a waterfall. The Nasdaq 100 is inches away from a bear market, now down 19.84% from the highs: Tech stocks are taking it on the chin. Four of the Mag 7 stocks are getting crushed right now: Nvidia is down almost 50% in a hurry. Luckily Apple is up almost 30% on the year and still less than 4% from all-time highs. That helps. It’s hard to believe but in the first week of October these were the year-to-date returns: Everything was going great. Now look at 2026 returns: That was fast. Boring old T-bills are now beating both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 this year: Ah, risk. Welcome back. Small caps, foreign developed stocks and emerging markets are also joining in on the fun: It’s not just the stock market that’s in some form of correction, bear market or crash right now. Gold and silver are both getting pummeled: The crypto complex too: I could keep going. Actually, let’s do a few more. Look at the 2x and 3x leveraged ETFs: Borrowed money is wonderful on the way up. It amplifies losses and emotions on the way down. Such is risk. Now if you really want to take risk these days you can also buy leveraged single stock ETFs. Look at how bombed out some of these 2x individual stock funds are: There are lots of other stocks, sectors, funds and strategies getting killed right now. I’m not one of those sadistic people that takes pleasure in the pain of others. A lot of investors are in a world of hurt right now. But allow me to make the case that this sell-off is a good thing. These are the returns in the previous three years for the S&P 500: And the Nasdaq 100: And oh by the way we are in like year 17 of an epic bull market. We were due for a reset. This is a healthy correction. It’s only a true risk if you don’t have a plan for how to survive it. Further Reading: When Will Buy the Dip Stop Working? Anthropic’s initial public offering netted the company over $81 billion on the first day of trading, making it one of, if not the, largest IPOs in history. The leading AI company, just five years old, now officially boasts a net worth in the neighborhood of $1.3-$1.7 trillion, depending on how you do your accounting. I think this is a good time, as such, to point out that, per a recent report, Anthropic also “has one of the worst recent records on fossil fuels, with analysis showing its upcoming data center projects could emit nearly 20 megatons of CO2-e a year.” Despite effectively positioning itself as a uniquely ethical AI company, Anthropic has been doubling down on fossil fuels to power its technology, both by turning to particularly polluting data centers, like xAI’s infamous Colossus plant in Memphis, for its compute needs, and embracing natural gas to power its own rapidly expanding array of in-house data centers.  Anthropic, of course, is not alone. Despite all the whipsawing AI news of late—Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia and failed comeback bid, the digital infrastructurapocalpyse of the last week, and the IPO, for starters—I was glad to see another study, on the climate impacts of the AI buildout, get some serious headlines. Even if those headlines were all of the ‘rather alarming’ variety, like the New York Times’, which went “Carbon Emissions of Biggest U.S. Data Centers Already Rival Entire Countries, Study Reveals.”  I was less glad to see BAAJA, a permitting reform bill designed to overturn key environmental protections in the name of making it easier for developers to build energy infrastructure and data centers, pass the Senate. We’ll get into all this, and a bit more, including a cameo from a very special guest who might help prove that data center skepticism runs in the family, in today’s edition. As always, this work is made possible by my magnificent paid subscribers—thank you, thank you—who chip in a few bucks a month so I can keep the lights on. If you’re able, and you find value in this work, please consider upgrading, too. Okay! Onwards. First, let’s get to that Harvard University study that made waves right before the Anthropic IPO. The report examined the CO2 emissions of over 400 of the United States’ largest data centers. It found that more than half of the power used to run them, 54%, was generated by fossil fuels, and thus, combined, they emitted as much carbon pollution as a mid-sized nation. Here’s the New York Times: The largest data centers in the United States are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually — almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark — according to new research. The study, published Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability, delivers the first peer-reviewed estimates of carbon dioxide emissions from the country’s biggest data centers since the start of the artificial intelligence boom. Its authors, a team led by researchers from Harvard University, examined the electricity consumption and carbon emissions of 403 data centers from May 2024 to April 2025. All told, those data centers used almost 2 percent of U.S. electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined, and represented about 0.5 percent of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions.  Now, if you think that finding sounds bad, then I hate to break it to you, but the actual emissions picture is probably much, much worse. For one thing, the survey ended in April of last year, and data center development has continued apace since then, with natural gas, and to a somewhat lesser extent, coal, supplying much of the new power demand. Furthermore, as Emily Atkin writes at her great climate newsletter HEATED, the study, for a number of key reasons, “gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution” data centers actually emit. From Atkin’s piece: One [issue] is the way the researchers counted the facilities’ emissions. To do this, they estimated how much electricity each data center used, then looked at how the grid in that part of the country makes its electricity—how much comes from gas, coal, renewables, and so on—to estimate how much CO₂ would be released to generate that much power. But not all data center electricity comes from the grid. Indeed, an ever-increasing number of these massive data centers are also building their own, on-site fossil fuel plants. For example, during the study period (May 2024 through April 2025), Elon Musk’s xAI got some of the electricity for its Colossus data center in Memphis from the grid—but it also got some of it by burning gas in turbines right outside the building. Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that Colossus wasn’t among the 403 facilities studied.  TLDR, the study doesn’t count the growing number of data centers, like Colossus, that use gas turbines on-site to power their plants. Furthermore, “electricity consumption is not the only way these facilities heat the planet. For example, the equipment that keeps the servers from overheating is leaking heat-trapping refrigerants into the atmosphere. And when a data center runs on gas—as so many of them do—methane can escape from wells and pipelines before the gas even reaches the power plant. Finally, due to their tracking methodology, the authors may have undercounted the number of data centers in operation at the time the study was carried out by a significant margin. As many as 250 data centers may be absent from the count, as of 2025, Atkin argues. All of which is to say, the study should be viewed as the floor; the minimum for how much greenhouse gas pollution data centers are emitting. And that is more than the entire country of Kenya. The findings of the Harvard study comport rather disconcertingly with those of another recent report, State of AI Climate Impact 2026, by the Australian climate researcher Ketan Joshi. Joshi’s report concludes that “The AI boom is already worsening greenhouse gas emissions,” and even more concerningly, that it is “potentially emitting more across its lifecycle than all international aviation.”  And, surprise, it’s only slated to get worse in coming years if current development patterns hold.  This is honestly pretty wild to contemplate here. The AI industry is on track, by some counts—including McKinsey’s—to generate more emissions than the coal mining industry, or global shipping and aviation. These are two of the most polluting heavy industries in the world, and AI is poised to blow past them. AI is already emitting twice the greenhouse gases of the global aluminum industry, itself a pretty crazy statistic given that aluminum production is a notoriously polluting endeavor. As the report states, “an unchecked continuation of these trends pushes the AI industry into becoming a major global heavy-emitting industry dwarfing both international aviation and international shipping.” Leading the way is the week’s big IPO winner, Anthropic. As I noted up top, Anthropic rose to prominence by burnishing a reputation as the most ethical purveyor of AI. This notably does not extend to environmental or climate concerns, arenas in which the leading AI firm is notably worse than almost all of its competition. Giants like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google may be reneging on their climate pledges, becoming less transparent in their emissions reporting, and diminishing their efforts to power servers and operations with clean energy. Meta, for instance, one of the nation’s largest data center operators, released its latest sustainability report this week, revealing that its emissions rose 45% since last year. The company said it was rethinking its erstwhile climate goals of producing net zero carbon emissions by 2030 as a result.  Yet Anthropic hasn’t even bothered to release any information about its carbon emissions or environmental impacts at all. Here’s a rundown from a special section of Joshi’s report focusing just on Anthropic and its posture towards energy and climate issues. It’s pretty damning. I’ll quote from it at length: Anthropic has never disclosed any energy, emissions or environmental data of any kind. In July 2025, Anthropic suggested the US government explicitly set a target for the construction of fossil gas power, promising to begin “preconstruction design work for natural gas plants” by the end of 2026. In May 2026, it was revealed that Anthropic is leasing capacity from the notoriously polluting SpaceX Memphis facility, itself a major source of local air pollution and climate pollution, and a project that has been strongly contested by affected locals; one analyst estimates (based on payments to SpaceX) that 1 in 2 Anthropic queries is served by this fossil-fueled facility (one of the worst in the world). In a recently released set of “data centre community commitments”, Anthropic promises much of the new power generation to serve their data centres will be “natural gas, which can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places we’re considering for data centers”. They claim to be considering renewable energy but do not provide any details, and promise to invest in carbon removal to “help address emissions”. In the S1 form filed by Anthropic, in advance of their Initial Public Offering (IPO), Anthropic suggests long term high emissions by declaring several fossil-fuel related risks, such as exposure to fossil fuel price volatility or competition with other customers for fossil gas. They also dismiss renewables as too high in cost (while ironically stating that “physical effects of climate change may increase our operating costs over time”). In November 2026, Anthropic struck a USD $3.4bn deal with OnePWR, a fossil fuelled turbine manufacturer, for 1.7 gigawatts of generators, with the Financial Times stating that the transaction “is the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab”. This transaction is more than three times the amount spent by xAI on its notoriously polluting Memphis turbines, and would emit approximately 6 MTCO2-e per year, equivalent to adding 1.8 million fossil-fuelled cars to the road. In November 2026, Anthropic posted a job listing paying up to $405,000 USD per year for “a Gas Supply & Transport Lead to own natural gas supply for Anthropic’s non-cloud data center portfolio in the United States and Canada”, adding that “if gas does not arrive, in the volume and at the pressure the plant needs, the compute does not run”. This is a clear portrait of a company that is not concerned with its own ballooning carbon emissions and climate impacts, until, that is, they threaten to hamper its data centers’ capacity to run smoothly.  The single biggest threat to AI data centers right now, however, is probably that everyone hates them. They hate them so much that public citizens across the United States have mobilized to shut them down, and elected politicians who’ve promised to help them do so. So how has the AI industry responded? By directing its trade groups and lobby to partner with the fossil fuel industry to push the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, through Congress before the data center-skeptical class of 2027 Democrats arrive. The tech industry is not just buying more fossil fuel power, it’s proactively working to enact policies that make it cheaper, easier and less democratic a process to build more fossil fuel power plants.  BAAJA is an assemblage of provisions the fossil fuels industry has been after for years: rollbacks on local governments’ legal tools to curtail development projects, curbs on endangered species protections, and a defanging of the Clean Water Act. Here’s Aaron Rugenberg, an environmental lawyer and the director of Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project, explaining in the New Republic:  BAAJA severely weakens the Clean Water Act, robbing states and tribes of their ability to protect water quality and require adequate safeguards for activities that pollute or destroy water resources. It practically nullifies the Endangered Species Act by delegating its core responsibilities to the states, most of which either oppose the act’s wildlife protections or lack the expertise and resources to adequately fulfill these obligations. And it essentially repeals the National Environmental Policy Act, the bedrock environmental law that gives the public a voice in decisions that impact the environment, by prohibiting the enforcement of NEPA violations. These three legal frameworks are responsible for most the improvements in water quality, green space, and wildlife recovery in our country over the last half-century. And that’s just the beginning. Other provisions of BAAJA go to even greater lengths to radically lock in fossil fuel development far into the future. The “disparate treatment” section of the bill effectively makes the permitting decisions of the Trump administration permanent. In the words of David Bookbinder, an environmental lawyer who has worked for both the left-leaning Sierra Club and the libertarian Niskanen Center, “The result of making these energy permitting policies permanent is that future administrations will be unable to effectively reduce GHG emissions.” BAAJA also guarantees not just the construction of fossil fuel projects but also their “operation at full capacity,” permanently blocking any future administration from regulating energy infrastructure. And it’s a similar case for data center projects. My friends at the AI Now Institute put out a statement declaring that a vote for BAAJA is “a vote for a ‘backdoor bailout’ of the AI industry.” Why? Two reasons: BAAJA preempts the few levers that local, state, and Tribal authorities have to hold Big Tech accountable. BAAJA supercharges AI data center expansion in exchange for token ratepayer protections. Coming as it is off the heels of the blue wave, anti-AI election, BAAJA feels like a slap in the face to voters. Or as Naomi Klein put it, “The voters just rejected data centers. Why is the Senate trying to fast-track them?” It’s crucial to note that this is not just a Republican/big tech/oil industry-led effort. A bunch of centrist and ‘abundance’ Democrats have joined the GOP in supporting the effort, under the auspices that it will cut red tape for clean energy projects, too. That’s true, to an extent, but this a terrible deal, and an absolutely unnecessary tradeoff at a point when Republicans’ stock could not be lower. After all, a) it’s just as important that we leave fossil fuels in the ground at this late stage of the climate crisis as it is that we build out more clean energy, and b) there are tools to effect desired outcomes without stripping local governments of the power to protect their communities and ecosystems.  Regardless, fast-track it the Senate did, with the help of more than a dozen Democratic Senators, including current Majority Leader Chuck Schumer. It now heads to the House of Representatives. I expect this to accelerate calls for a change in Senate leadership.  To recap: As of spring in 2025, American data centers were emitting as much greenhouse gas pollution as nations like Kenya, Bolivia, and Denmark. They are almost certainly emitting much more than that today. Worldwide, the AI industry is on a trajectory to outpace the emissions of the heaviest and most-polluting industries, like aviation and coal mining, within the next ten years. And tech firms are fighting to make it easier and faster to build more fossil fuel projects and data centers. In other words, the AI industry is quickly becoming not just a concern, but something more akin to a disaster for the climate. It’s no longer merely prolonging the lifespan of fossil fueled power plants, but actively working to bring more of them online to run their data centers, at a scale that was mostly unthinkable even three years ago.  “There’s a kind of dirty ‘energy desperation’ within the industry,” the climate researcher and study author Ketan Joshi tells me. “If you give them 100 wind farms, they’ll take those but still build 5 city-sized gas plants, because the brute force software system they provide has no upper limit on energy consumption.” ”What this means is that regulation that aims to treat the symptoms (eg: 100% renewable mandates, or deregulating permitting to allow for more transmission) just gets added on top of AI consumption,” he adds. “Like fossil fuels in general, we need to limit the source.” There’s one more element to all of this that needs to be underlined, and that’s the fact that the AI industry’s data center and fossil fuel infrastructure buildout won’t just contribute to carbon emissions, but air pollution, too. There’s a real cost to respiratory health, and not just to those who live close to next door to polluting mega-projects like xAI’s Colossus.  Dr. Robert Merchant is a pulmonologist in Montana, where a massive 8 square mile data center project has begun construction, built by Quantica Infrastructure, outside of Billings. The project involves bringing online gas-fired power plants to provide 1,800 megawatts of capacity—more capacity than all other power plants currently operating in Montana combined. Merchant submitted a study of the respiratory health impacts a power plant of that size to Yellowstone County, and spoke at a public meeting with the commissioners. Merchant, who I might add is my uncle, and thus perhaps is evidence of a familial predisposition to taking data center interests to task, noted how this level of gas-fired power generation will loose particulate pollution across the state and far beyond. Based on his modeling, the data center project would increase asthma rates, illness rates, as well as the number of heart attacks and strokes. It would cost between $20-50 million in medical costs, dampen productivity in the region as workers take more sick days, and cause 1-2 deaths per year. His report and presentation made news in the local media. Here’s the Montana Free Press: Robert Merchant, a semi-retired Billings Clinic doctor, presented his findings at the commissioners’ Thursday discussion meeting… Fine particles containing nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, methane and other gases can contribute to asthma, heart attacks, cancer, low birthweight, cognitive functioning and other health problems, he wrote. Merchant said the environmental impacts from the data center, as currently planned, would spill well beyond Yellowstone County, stretching as far south as northern Texas… “Inaction will result in health and economic damage to the public.” Merchant thanked the commissioners for their work and said he hoped the data he shared was useful to their analysis. Merchant’s presentation was met with applause.   Get ‘em, uncle Bob.  I used my inside connections to reach out to Merchant and ask if there was anything about his report or the situation in Montana he wanted to share with readers. He responded in kind: What frustrates me to no end is that this type of data isn’t part of every single proposal for a new data center. What a complete lack of transparency. Even if they don’t do the modeling of health effects they should be required to state their expected emissions. I had to reach out to acquaintances at an excellent organization, Montana Environmental Information Center, to get the needed estimates. They gathered it up for public, but not easily found, information. A reporter from our local paper had also sourced some of the information. It wasn’t that hard for me to do the analysis and report but why should the region be relying on a retired pulmonologist to figure out the health impacts of this huge new data center? Where is the EPA? Where is the Montana Department of Environmental Quality? Where is the Yellowstone County Public Health Department? Or even more idealistically, shouldn’t the company itself care about the region and do the analysis themselves? And share it with the community? I could not agree more. Speaking of, this kind of transparency would be some very low-hanging fruit that the new wave of data center-critical politicians could demand when they take office. The AI industry and its data center buildout are on track to become a genuine crisis factor for the climate, especially given its limitless appetite for expansion. And it’s funny, you never hear the AI execs promise that their products are going to “solve” climate change anymore. Now they stick to saying it will cure cancer. Saying AI is good for climate now apparently creates too much cognitive dissonance for the tech elite to stomach, and that’s saying something.  Some fun media stuff this week:  I joined KQED’s Forum with Washington Post tech reporter Shira Ovide and former Biden AI policy advisor Ben Buchanan. We talked Nvidia, Anthropic, the global internet outages, and more. It’s always a good time joining Alexis’s show.  I was interviewed for the BBC’s Global Story, for an episode about AI and Luddites, which was particularly cool.  It’s n+1 Bookmatch season, which longtime readers know is one of my favorite holiday traditions. If you haven’t taken it yet, get to it; donate to a great literary mag and find some stellar reads in the process. I got at least one home run already, which I somehow missed until now: Matthew Wolfe’s Fires in the Night, a history of the Earth Liberation Front, a group with some strong Luddite vibes indeed.  Finally, if you didn’t catch it, for the show this week I sat down with Cory Doctorow to talk about how AI is breaking the internet. This is already one of our biggest shows on YouTube, for perhaps the obvious reasons. No one does this better than Cory.  Alright, that’s it for now. As always, thanks for reading. And keep those hammers up.   Just a reminder that this is a space for human commentary and discussion, and AI-generated comments will be deleted. Remember how we were promised just three years ago that AI would solve climate change? You don't hear much of that anymore...

By Melanie Goodfellow  Senior International Film Correspondent  	Expectations that a new Avengers: Doomsday teaser or trailer is imminent have hit fever pitch over the weekend following cast member Hayley Atwell’s omission while signing autographs in New York that it is dropping on Monday (November 23).  	“There’s a new trailer dropping on Monday… am I allowed to have said that?” Atwell, who returns to the franchise as Peggy Carter, told fans on Friday night.  	Disney has also announced a sneak peek for November 30 during The Wonderful World of Disney: Holiday Spectacular on ABC, but this is believed to be a different tease.      	 	 		 					Related Stories		 	              	News 	    	 		 					Watermelon Expands Production Ambitions As It Seals Partnership With Qatar's Film Committee		 			                	News 	    	 		 					Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days		 			        	A few hours prior to Atwell’s omission, some 7,000 miles away in Qatar, co-director Joe Russo had also hinted at fresh drops before the picture’s opening by Disney on December 18, telling fans to keep checking their feeds.  	           			Watch on Deadline		       	Talking in a fireside chat at the Qatar Film Committee’s second Doha Industry Days, Russo explained that the four teasers, preceding an official trailer this summer, had played an integral role in the final version of the film.  	He said it had been a way to connect with the fans, which was essential because the audience landscape had changed so much since Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame in 2018 and 2019 respectively.  	“I have to work extra hard to subvert your expectations and be aware of who you are as a viewer and how you’re changing,” said Russo.  	“The last time I did this, in 2018, 2019, is very different than now because we’ve been through a pandemic; lots of people spent a lot of time on social media. Movies saw a tremendous downturn, streaming saw a tremendous upturn, and now that all seems to be reversing. So, it shifts constantly,” he said. “You have to be a futurist to try to predict where the market is going.”  	“I have to interact with the fans in order to understand what is moving them, what is working for them,” he said. “What we’ve been doing with Doomsday is very different than the last time we did this because the speed of conversation on the internet is even faster than it was in 2018, 2019.”  	           	“I had this idea, why don’t we start the story a year early? Why don’t we start dropping clues in the year leading up to the movie… we did four trailers that were sprinkled out,” he continued.  	Kicking off on December 23, 2025, the first trailer showing Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) returning home, unpacking his Captain America suit, and holding a baby. A teaser on November 30 showed Thor (Chris Hemsworth) praying to Odin for strength. This was followed onJanuary 6 2026 drop featuring the X-Men and a January 13 teaser, featuring the Wakandans and Fantastic Four.  	“We’ve done a series of tags around the characters because the story actually started in January of last year, and you’ve been watching it slowly unfold and these are all pieces of something that are going to equal two and a half hours of your time on December 18,” he said.  	“It’s slowly investing them [fans] emotionally. But I’m also getting feedback as that’s happening and we can make adjustments as we go, based on what people are tracking or not tracking,” he continued.  	“It’s a very complicated story also, so I have to make sure that they’re following each little crumb we give them. If they get the wrong thing from it, then I have to make adjustments, knowing that they might have the wrong idea about it.”  	Talking about his return to the Avengers franchise alongside brother Anthony Russo, Joe Russo said he had been reluctant at first because of the immense challenge of pulling off a Marvel movie at that scale.  	He credited Robert Downey Jr., who played Tony Stark/Iron Man in Avengers: Endgame, with planting the seed for a return to the franchise, with his revelation that he was down to play Victor von Doom/Doctor Doom.  	“He’s a very dear friend of mine, but I also think he’s the greatest actor of his generation. This is a supremely talented, charismatic human being. And he translates incredibly well on a global scale. There’s something about the nature of his performance that translates,” said Russo.  	“There’s a style that belongs to these films that allows them to work in every market around the world. He just embodies that,” he said.  	Russo said Robert had gently enquired whether he was up for coming back to the Avengers franchise over dinner a couple of years ago.  	“I was still recovering from Infinity War and Endgame. And I was hesitant… he’s smart, he doesn’t push too much, he just kind of dropped the idea on the table and let it sit there, and then after dinner, he brought it up again, and I was like, ‘I don’t think I could do it, I’m still too tired.’ And then this festered for a little bit. And he didn’t even really tell me what he was going to do going back,” recall Russo.  	“And then another conversation happened where he said, ‘You know, I’m going to play Doom’. And I said, ‘That’s a really clever idea”. I can see a corollary there. There are thematics, greatest hero, greatest villain. There’s a multiverse. There’s a reason for being. There’s a compelling idea there. And I went, ‘Well, of course, who else could play the greatest villain other than you.”  	“It started to simmer in my brain a little bit. But we didn’t have a story. You can’t just show up with an empty canvas, so I still said no.”  	Russo credited longtime collaborator, screenwriter Steve McFeely, with coming up with the premise that gave a way in to writing Doomsday, after they had been pitching ideas back and forth.  	           	“Steve McFeely called me and said, ‘I have a crazy idea about how this works… what would happen if you left the cameras rolling at the end of Endgame? What’s the very next scene that happens,” recounted Russo.  	“I said, “That’s really risky for a movie that had the level of success it did. You’re going to impact people’s emotional investment in it… this could blow up in your face,’ and then I went, ‘I love it’,” he continued.  	“The concept was like that’s a very happy ending for one character. And what if happiness is finite, and what if you have to take happiness from someone else to create your own happiness… What happens in that story? That’s where I went, ‘Right, I know what to do with this.” The idea that like there was a cost to a happy ending.” Get our Breaking News Alerts and Keep your inbox happy. Author of the Small Business Insider newsletter Giving out free coffee might not sound like a winning business strategy. For Brandon Sardi, the founder of San Francisco-based Poorboy Coffee, it became a way to market his company and put money in another entrepreneur's pocket. Poorboy started with pop-ups at wine bars. Sardi did hundreds of them during the company's first couple of years, but the business model was tough to justify: He and his team would spend hours preparing, hauling equipment, setting up, and hoping enough people would stop by for a $5 drink. Then Poorboy moved into private catering, where clients pay in advance. The economics were better, Sardi said, and he largely stopped doing public pop-ups — but he missed the community-facing side of the business. That's where "Who Gives a Hand" comes in: a new pay-what-you-want pop-up series. Customers can take a drink for free or contribute whatever amount they choose. Every dollar collected is passed directly to another local small business. "It's a way for us to be creative as far as marketing goes," Sardi told Business Insider. "I want people to hear more about Poorboy, and especially in a good light." Sardi held the first Who Gives a Hand event at a former Poorboy pop-up location. He expected the prospect of free drinks, combined with promotion on social media, to draw a crowd. He was surprised when no line formed. The event was slow — a familiar feeling from Poorboy's earlier pop-up days — but the customers who did show up were generous. Sardi said nearly everyone contributed, with some paying more than they would have for a typical drink and others giving as much as $50.
