He set up a live tracker showing the total, which helped entice people to add to the pot. Over three hours, the event collected $957 in pay-it-forward contributions — more than double the roughly $450 in sales he said a typical pop-up brought in. Sardi passed the money on to the owners of AK Meats, a family-run San Francisco business. A post shared by Brandon Sardi | Behind the scenes of building a business (@brandonsardi) The second event produced a different result.  Although roughly as many people stopped by, more took their drinks without paying — which Sardi said was completely within the spirit of the model. He suspects some customers didn't fully understand the concept, but the experience didn't discourage him. Sardi is planning more pop-ups, including one in New York City. While not as successful as the first, the second event still collected about $500. Sardi's staff declined payment for their time, wanting to contribute to the pay-it-forward effort themselves. Sardi added another $500 of his own money so Poorboy could again pass $1,000 along to another local business. There are real costs to staging the events: ingredients, transportation, staff time, and a full day of work. Still, he sees the exchange as worthwhile. Customers get a good coffee and the freedom to decide what it's worth. Poorboy gets an opportunity to introduce itself to potential customers and build goodwill. And a local small business receives a no-strings-attached cash infusion. "It's kind of like a win-win-win in every sense," he said. For Sardi, who started Poorboy with about $500, the final piece matters most. He knows how difficult it can be to bootstrap an idea and hopes the gesture can help another owner keep going. "To be able to, after the pop-up, give that chunk of change to someone and make someone's day and see their reaction," he said, "it's kind of priceless." Jump to

Contact us by Email Nov. 22 2026, Published 7:00 a.m. ET On a trip to New York City in 1950, Judy Garland ducked into a late-night screening of Summer Stock, her third musical co-starring Gene Kelly, at a Times Square theater, RadarOnline.com can reveal.  "After the film, she exited the theater to thunderous applause," said film expert David Fantle. "Cheering fans followed her to her car, which had to give her a warm feeling because she'd been away from the screen for over a year." Judy Garland recommended Gene Kelly to the studio after seeing him in Broadway's 'Pal Joey.' Summer Stock, which included Garland's showstopping number "Get Happy," might never have made it to the big screen without the support of her great friend Kelly.  The book C'mon, Get Happy: The Making of Summer Stock by Fantle and Tom Johnson tells the story behind the film and shares new details of Garland and Kelly's special friendship. Garland first laid eyes on Kelly singing and dancing in Pal Joey, which debuted on Broadway in 1940.  She was very impressed. "She recommended Gene to the studio before anyone knew who he was," Johnson said. Kelly would make his movie debut opposite Garland two years later in 1942's For Me and My Gal, where she took the film novice under her wing on set. "She would never take credit for any of Gene's success. She just thought he was fantastic and should be given a shot in movies," Johnson explains. The two powerhouse performers became off-set friends, too. "They went out pub-crawling in Montana when she was there on a short vacation," saidJohnson, who adds that Judy became a frequent guest at the Beverly Hills home Kelly shared with his first wife, Betsy. 'Summer Stock' was initially intended to reunite Garland with Mickey Rooney. "She spent a lot of weekends playing volleyball and singing [with them] all through the '40s and into the '50s," he noted. Kelly and Garland's third movie together, Summer Stock, a variation of the let's-put-on-a-show musical, was initially intended as a vehicle to reunite her with Mickey Rooney. "They all thought [Summer Stock] was a throwback," Johnson said. "Initially, when they were doing it, they all thought it was a piece of c--p – even Judy." Meanwhile, the star's personal problems had begun to mount.  By the start of production, Judy's marriage to Vincente Minnelli was in tatters and her dependency on prescription drugs was impacting her health, emotions and weight, which visibly fluctuated in the film. Kelly, along with director Charles Walters and several other longtime friends at MGM, vowed to help her complete filming. "Gene famously said, 'I don't care if it takes a year. I will stay here and be here for her,'" Johnson recalled. That generosity might surprise fans who only know of Kelly's reputation as a perfectionist taskmaster, but Judy brought out a different side. "She wouldn't suffer fools, and you also couldn't bully her," Johnson said. Share article Print article For many Australians, watching a football match means more than following the score and supporting your team. There are betting odds, promotions and invitations to turn sporting knowledge into a wager. Betting on sport isn’t new. But its routine place in watching and following sport is relatively recent, and the sports betting industry helped build that relationship. On January 1 2027, new federal rules will restrict gambling advertising. The government says it wants to break the link between wagering and sport. But betting companies have spent years helping make that link seem natural. The stakes are enormous. According to the government’s impact analysis, Australians lost A$32.2 billion on legal gambling in 2023-24 – about $1,521 per adult and the highest per-capita losses in the world. Of that, $8.4 billion was lost betting on racing and sport. Gambling companies in Australia have invested heavily in advertising to reach audiences. Spending rose from $89.7 million in 2011 to $287.2 million in 2021, according to published research. That’s more than triple, excluding sponsorship and advertising within programs. The scale is extraordinary. Australia’s communications regulator counted more than one million gambling advertisements on free-to-air television and metropolitan radio in just 12 months to April 2023. Half of those promoted online gambling. Advertising has since declined. The government’s analysis shows television wagering ads fell by 53% between 2022 and 2024. But years of exposure have left a cultural legacy. A 2020 New South Wales study of 12 to 17-year-olds found 31% considered sports betting normal, while 15% regarded knowing the odds as part of following sport. In a national survey published in 2023, 69% of adults believed gambling advertising makes betting seem like a normal part of sport. These findings reveal how familiar betting has become, even to people too young to gamble legally. A bipartisan 2023 parliamentary inquiry, chaired by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, unanimously recommended a comprehensive online gambling advertising ban, to be phased in over three years. After taking three years to respond, the federal government passed more limited reforms in August this year. From January 1, betting advertising will be banned from sporting venues and uniforms, while athletes, celebrities and influencers cannot promote wagering. Advertising during live sport will face tighter restrictions. But television can still carry three betting ads per hour between 5am and 8.30pm, except around live sport and during children’s programs. Online platforms can also advertise to verified adults who are logged in, unless they deliberately choose to opt out. These are meaningful changes, but they fall short of the inquiry’s comprehensive recommendations.          Read more:       Long-awaited gambling reform bill is an improvement, but does not go nearly far enough to reduce harm    Here’s the less obvious part of the story. Businesses don’t simply compete within existing markets. They can reshape markets by changing what people buy, how they buy it, who participates, and what people consider normal. Researchers call this “market shaping”. Market shaping isn’t necessarily a bad thing. In one piece of research, we examined how New Zealand winemakers challenged the belief that premium wine needed a cork, helping make screwcaps acceptable on premium wines and reducing problems associated with faulty corks.  But our recent research on disposable packaging shows how US plastics and beverage industries helped normalise throwaway containers, while shifting responsibility for waste onto local governments and consumers. Sports betting provides another example. Apps made placing bets easier. Advertising and betting odds helped present wagering as part of sporting participation. Sponsorships connected bookmakers financially with clubs, broadcasters and sporting codes.  A 2026 investigation found every National Rugby League club and five Australian Football League clubs had gambling sponsors. These changes reinforce one another. As betting became familiar to audiences, it became more commercially valuable to broadcasters and sporting organisations. Their growing dependence on that betting revenue, in turn, encouraged its continued promotion. Those relationships now complicate reform. In its assessment of the options, the government estimated a full advertising ban would deliver an annual net benefit of $217.6 million, double the $107.1 million from its more limited restrictions. These benefits would mainly come from reduced gambling losses and associated health, psychological, financial and relationship harms. However, broadcasters argued that gambling advertising helps fund their services, including free-to-air news and public-interest journalism. They warned losing this revenue could threaten news services, particularly in regional Australia. Sporting organisations raised similar concerns about funding for grassroots sport. The government acknowledged it could not reliably quantify these potential consequences. Nevertheless, these concerns influenced its decision to adopt the narrower approach. Here is the paradox: the commercial deals and associated advertising revenue that helped make betting normal have themselves become arguments against stronger reform. Restricting advertising is a start. But changing the market means changing its habits, financial relationships and shared expectations. The federal government could revisit the inquiry’s proposal for a phased comprehensive ban while helping clubs, sporting codes and broadcasters replace betting-related income. For example, public funding could temporarily replace gambling sponsorships, potentially financed through a levy on betting companies. There is a precedent: beginning in 1987, VicHealth used tobacco-tax revenue to help replace tobacco sponsorship of sport and the arts. Western Australia later established Healthway for similar purposes. Regulators should also monitor whether promotion shifts into other channels and whether young Australians continue to associate betting with sport. Ultimately, success should not be measured simply by how many advertisements disappear. It should be measured by whether gambling stops feeling like an ordinary part of following sport. To break the connection between gambling and sport, we must change more than the advertising. We must change the market that makes it valuable. This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Economist Adam Smith spoke of free markets, with prices being determined by the forces of demand and supply. But markets seldom operate in a textbook manner and there is overbearing oversight driven by different motivations.  At one end are stock markets. All stock prices are determined by the forces of demand and supply. While there are circuit breakers to check extreme price movements, business carries on after the scheduled breaks. There is a regulatory structure that lays down the rules, but there is no price view.  It is probably the only market where higher prices are welcomed by everyone. Governments take it as a vindication of their policies. Companies believe it reflects their true market value, and shareholders and traders are happy that they are making money.  At the other end is the commodity market, which is segmented. Prices for manufactured products are decided by the producers, and there is little interference except in the case of food products such as sugar or edible oils. Companies look at market conditions and weigh their options and take a call on prices. These are strategic decisions taken after considering how others would react.   The agricultural markets are ambivalent. There are some that fall under the category of crops where there are minimum support prices (MSPs) set by the government. These set a floor. This works well for rice and wheat but not for other crops where there is no procurement. A price fall can affect the income of farmers when there are oversupplies. There are essential commodities whose prices are remotely controlled by the government. Low output of sugar or tur dal can make the government impose stock limits to curb hoarding at the wholesale and retail levels. These limits are puzzling as typically all crops involve single-season harvests. This means that someone has to buy at the time of harvest and store for the next 12 months to ensure the produce is available.  Farmers do not have holding power and sell their crop at the time of harvest. But these intermediaries run the risk of censure and imprisonment for violation of these limits. There is hence an explicit conflict in supporting the farmers through MSPs and protecting the consumer with fair prices.  Moving away from crops to non-crops, which include horticulture, prices are determined by market forces. Onion prices often rise as high as  ₹120 a kilogram and the farmers benefit, or tomato prices sometimes crash to less than  ₹1 a kilogram and farmers are forced to dump the produce on the roads as the cost of transport exceeds the price. There is seldom intervention here in price discovery, though policies can induce imports to lift supplies.   The more complex market is of currencies. There is a view that market forces should determine the exchange rate with little interference. But central banks cannot sit back and let the rupee depreciate endlessly as it affects external stability. For instance, unbridled depreciation will increase the cost of imports and affect inflation and hence monetary policy. A weakening rupee will cause foreign investors to keep away, which will hasten the depreciation.  Therefore, there has to be intervention. At times, central banks take decisions keeping in mind what other central banks are doing to maintain competitive advantage in trade.  This presents a conundrum for the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The market tries to guess the number that RBI has in mind. Presently, from revealed action, it is believed that  ₹97 to a dollar is a threshold. Hence, everyone takes positions based on such conjectures. RBI acts in the spot market or takes forward positions or in extreme cases brings in the big-bang Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposit scheme to ensure discipline. Therefore, this market seems to be quite regulated.    The last is the bond market. Here, there seems to be a view that ideally the bond yields should be low as it supports the government’s borrowing programme. Market makers play along and ensure there is liquidity in the benchmark bonds. Liquidity levels are monitored closely by RBI to stabilize bond yields as the central bank is also a banker to the government.  These yields are globally aligned. High oil prices drive them up. Similarly, higher US bond yields put upward pressure on these rates to align. The market calculates the spread between US treasuries and our bonds. While there is no science to these numbers, a long-term difference of 250 basis points is taken to be normal. This also needs monitoring. Hence, it is very hard to let markets determine prices because of the interlinkages across segments. Also, there is a case of striking a balance between consumer and farmer interest. Currency and bonds have implications for the macro-economy and cannot be ignored.  It is also not surprising that we view certain market players differently based on the markets they operate in: market makers are good in bonds but are called speculators in others and are not trusted. Intermediaries are required to hold and supply goods but not hoard. But if there were only hedgers, then price discovery would never take place. Therein lies the rub.  These are the author’s personal views. Lazy imports are having a moment. Python 3.15 adds a lazy import statement, from PEP 810, and a module can name imports it wants deferred in a __lazy_modules__ list. A deferred import binds its name straight away, but the module isn't loaded until the code first uses it. Most of the excitement is about command line tools. A tool which imports everything it might ever need, just to print its --help, can start in a fraction of the time when most of those imports are deferred. A web application served by a pre-forking server is a different calculation, and deferring imports there can make things worse rather than better. Whether it helps depends on the application, on how it is deployed, and on what its requests actually use, which is why Muru measures imports rather than leaving it to guesswork. As covered in the import once, fork many post, Muru imports an application once in a host process, and forks the workers from it. Everything the host imported is shared by the workers through copy on write memory, and is paid for once. Under the Muru daemon, a deploy starts a new release beside the one serving, as covered in the releases, not restarts post, and traffic only moves to it once it is ready. However long the new release takes to import the application, nobody visiting the site waits for it. Deferring an import doesn't save anyone any time there. What it does is move the cost into the first request in each worker which uses the module, and since each worker then loads the module itself, its memory is no longer shared. Under muructl serve in a container, a new release is a new container, and the import is part of how long it takes to start. A shorter start makes a rollout or a scale-out finish sooner. Even so, as covered in the working with Kubernetes post, Muru's readiness probe doesn't pass until the application is loaded and the workers are ready, so a new pod still gets no requests before it can serve them. There are times when someone does wait for the import. A release scaled to zero with its host stopped makes the next request wait for the host to start and import the application. And muructl run in development loads the application again every time a file changes. So a deferred import can help or hurt, depending on how the application is run and how often its requests use what was deferred. To decide, it helps to know what each import costs, and what the workers end up loading anyway. The example for this post is a small Flask shop with two features that need large libraries. A stock report uses pandas: and a download of the stock list as a spreadsheet uses openpyxl: Someone has already tried to keep start-up fast, so the view for the report imports shop.reports inside the function, while shop.export is imported at the top of the application's module like everything else: It runs under muructl run with two worker processes, on Python 3.14. Muru can record every import the host makes while it loads the application, using the profile recorder of unwrapt, a package for lazy imports which I wrote alongside Muru. With unwrapt added to the project's dependencies, import_report turns it on: muructl debug imports then prints a report of the host's load: Most of the load was openpyxl. The advice for each import says what deferring it would mean, and the configuration to write. For the shop's own code, that is a __lazy_modules__ list in the module making the import. For an import inside a package the project depends on, where nobody wants to edit the package's source, it is an entry of unwrapt's [tool.unwrapt.lazy_modules] table, naming the importing module and what to defer in it. The first piece of advice is about the application's own from shop import export, and nearly all of its 71.2 milliseconds is the openpyxl which shop.export imports, so the two are different ways of deferring the same cost. The 3.15 and UNWRAPT columns say whether each way of deferring can defer that import as written, since Python 3.15 can defer a from import while unwrapt can only defer a plain import. On the Python 3.14 the shop runs on, deferring the from import would save nothing unless it were rewritten, which is why its SAVES column is zero. The report lists by default only the imports there is something to do about. With --all it lists the rest, among them the numpy which openpyxl imports in turn, for 28.6 of openpyxl's milliseconds: It isn't advised, because openpyxl.compat.numbers uses numpy at the top level, straight after importing it, to build a tuple of numeric types. A deferred import that is used the moment it is made is loaded straight away anyway, so deferring it would save nothing. The same report comes from muructl check --imports, which loads the application once without serving anything, so it can be run before and after a change, or in CI. The spreadsheet export is used rarely, so deferring openpyxl looks worthwhile. That takes two changes. The module names the import in __lazy_modules__, before the import itself: and the project turns on lazy_imports: Python 3.15 and later act on __lazy_modules__ by themselves. Python 3.11 to 3.14 ignore it, and with lazy_imports on, Muru has unwrapt defer the imports it names instead, so the same code defers on every version of Python Muru supports. The lazy import statement can't be used that way, since it is a syntax error before 3.15. As the host forks, it says what was deferred, and whether anything used a deferred import before the fork anyway, in which case deferring it saved nothing: How much this saved needs more than one measurement, since a load's time varies from one start to the next by about as much as the difference being measured. A muru.local.toml beside the project overrides the project's settings for my own runs only, so lazy_imports = false in it turns deferral off without changing pyproject.toml. With import_report = false there as well, since recording the imports adds to the load, I started the run five times each way. The host took a median of 83 milliseconds to load the application without deferral, and 35 milliseconds with it. The cost hasn't gone away though, it has moved. The first request for the spreadsheet in a worker now loads openpyxl, and the numpy it imports in turn: The import entry in Server-Timing is the time the request spent loading modules for the first time in its worker. The request's Timing panel, on the dashboard here since a spreadsheet has no page for the toolbar, shows it as an "importing modules" row, and its list of the modules loaded marks the one that resolved a deferred import, with the line of code that first used it:  Line 11 of shop/export.py is book = openpyxl.Workbook(), the first use of the module. Since numpy was a good part of that, I tried deferring it inside openpyxl anyway, to see what the report's reason for not advising it looks like in practice, with an entry of [tool.unwrapt.lazy_modules]: The list of modules for the next first download showed numpy (deferred) being loaded from line 16 of openpyxl/compat/numbers.py, while openpyxl itself was still loading. That is the line which builds the tuple of numeric types, so the deferred import was used the moment it was made. The workers' part of muructl debug imports, which comes up next, said the same of it, "used as openpyxl.compat.numbers loads, at openpyxl/compat/numbers.py:16; deferring it saves nothing, remove the entry", so I took the entry out again. Whether moving that cost was worth it depends on how many workers end up paying it, and that depends on the traffic. After the run had served some pages, several stock reports and one spreadsheet, the last part of muructl debug imports asked each worker what it had loaded for the first time since the fork: The two features come out on opposite sides. Only one worker had needed openpyxl, so the other was spared both the time and the memory, and the deferral paid off. Every worker had needed shop.reports, and each loaded pandas itself, about 135 milliseconds a time, which the function level import in the view had pushed into the first report each worker served. That first report is also worse than it looks. With three requests for the report sent at once, two of them went to the same worker on different threads, and both took about 140 milliseconds. Only one of them was loading pandas. The other was waiting on Python's import lock for it to finish, and their Server-Timing headers tell the two apart: The second request's Timing panel has a "waiting for an import" row in place of "importing modules", and names the module and the request it was waiting on: The first requests after a deploy, or after a scale-out adds workers, are exactly when that happens. A module that every worker loads is better loaded once, in the host, before the fork. preload_modules lists modules for the host to import after the application, as part of the same load: The host's load now includes pandas, and the first reports in each worker took from four and a half to nine milliseconds, rather than more than a hundred. The import report gives the entry's own cost on a line of its own, preload_modules entry shop.reports: 145.5 ms in the host, and doesn't advise deferring anything the entry loads, since that would only undo it. preload_modules is also the way to undo a deferral you don't want. Once Python 3.15 is common, libraries will start using lazy import themselves, for their own command line tools or their own start-up time, and in a web application that may move a library's import into the first request of each worker. Listing the module in preload_modules loads it before the fork regardless, and the deferred import finds it already loaded when the code first uses it. The advice is only as good as the traffic the workers have seen. After a few more downloads of the spreadsheet, both workers had served one: With two workers running for a long time, a module that any request uses at all eventually ends up loaded in all of them, at which point the deferral bought nothing but a slower first request in each. With more workers, workers that are replaced after a number of requests, or an autoscaler which adds and removes workers as load changes, many workers may never get as far as needing it. Which of those describes a production deployment is something only its own traffic can say, so this is a question to ask of a running release rather than a development run. The same counts are kept as metrics, muru_worker_modules_loaded_total and muru_worker_module_load_seconds_total, so they can be watched over time. Lazy imports are a useful tool, but in a web application served by a pre-forking server they are a trade between the host's load, the first request in each worker, and how much memory the workers share. Muru gives you the measurements to make that trade for your own application. The Server-Timing header and the Timing panel show what a request paid for imports, the import report shows what the host's load costs and where to cut it, and the workers say what they ended up loading anyway. Deferral through unwrapt works the same from Python 3.11 to 3.15, and preload_modules puts back what shouldn't have been deferred. The next post, working with coding agents, is about something else doing things through Muru. Coding agents are increasingly the ones running, deploying and debugging applications, and Muru gives them a way in through MCP, so an agent can deploy each change as a release, read the events, logs and worker stacks when something fails, and roll back, using everything the earlier posts covered.
